scope: Paper-relationship re-reviews of the 34 pre-expansion tasks upgraded with an evaluator (validation/prize-expansion/evaluator-upgrades.json): whether the primary paper evaluates the named benchmark, problem or objective, where it says so, and every difference between that experiment and the local task.
method: For each task the cached primary paper text (.cache/primary-paper-text, digests below) was read around the experiments, benchmarks, metrics and appendices and compared with the task manifest, problem contract, upgrade notes and local evaluator modules. Evidence passages are identified by the SHA-256 of their whitespace-normalised text and their offset in that text; the passages themselves are not redistributed.

source_associations.locator: Section 4.2 Domains (Paper review); Appendix C.2 Paper Review; Section 5.1; Appendix D.1 Table 3
source_associations.finding: HyperAgents evaluates a paper-review domain in which an agent reads the full text of an AI research paper and predicts accept/reject, scored by classification accuracy against observed ICLR 2024/2025 and NeurIPS 2023/2024 decisions, with 100-task train/validation/test splits drawn from Zhao et al. (2026). The local task reuses Hyperagents' released dataset and split script and scores lower-cased exact-match accuracy on a 20-paper subsample of the test split with a free-form solve program instead of the evolved DGM-H agents.

findings: Benchmark: the paper's paper-review domain (full paper text -> binary accept/reject, classification accuracy vs. observed decisions, data from Zhao et al. (2026), i.e. APRES) is the benchmark the task names. The 711-paper dataset.csv, the balanced 50/50 test split and the curation script come from the Hyperagents repository, not the paper; the paper only says the splits are randomly sampled with 100 tasks each. Identity of the locally recomputed test split with the authors' split is not verified (disclosed).

Sample size: the local score is accuracy on a fixed 20-paper subsample of the 100-paper test split (granularity 0.05, high variance); the paper reports medians over 5 runs with 95% bootstrap CIs on the full 100 test tasks (e.g. DGM-H 0.710, CI 0.590-0.750). Sample size disclosed; the 0.710 figure quoted in the notes matches Section 5.1 and is not reproduced (disclosed).

Model: the paper's paper-review task evaluation uses GPT-4o at temperature 0.0 (self-modification by Claude 4.5 Sonnet; Appendix D.1 Table 3). The local default is google/gemini-2.5-flash at temperature 0; the local model is disclosed but the notes do not name the paper's evaluation model.

Candidate: the paper evolves task-agent and meta-agent code (DGM-H, 100 iterations, staged evaluation on 10 then 100 training tasks, parent selection on the validation split, best agent tested once). Locally a free-form solve(question, llm) program is scored directly on test papers under a USD 0.25 per-evaluation budget; no train/validation data is exposed. Disclosed.

Scoring: the accuracy rule (strip + lower-case exact match against the decision) matches Hyperagents' domains/report.py at the pinned commit, which compares an already-extracted 'prediction' field and drops rows whose prediction is empty. The answer-extraction step in the contract ('Answer:' marker, else \boxed{}, else last line) is the suite's generic llm_bench_core.final_answer rule, not Hyperagents' (there, the evolvable task agent itself produces the prediction), yet the contract labels the whole rule "Hyperagents' check".

Prompt: the local question wraps the paper text with an instruction and 'Answer accept or reject'; Hyperagents' initial agent receives the raw input (and scores 0.0 because it lacks output parsing). This added instruction is disclosed for the IMO task but not for this task.

Unverified observation: Appendix D.2 estimates 0.5M GPT-4o tokens to evaluate 100 paper-review tasks (about 5k tokens per paper), which is hard to reconcile with the ~74,000-character (about 18k-token) full texts in the local data; the paper does not say whether paper texts were truncated, so input-length parity with the paper cannot be confirmed.

applied_corrections: Corrected after this review: The paper's evaluation model for this domain (GPT-4o, temperature 0.0) is not named in the notes; only the local default model is stated.

Corrected after this review: The answer-extraction rule ('Answer:' / \boxed{} / last line) is a local convention attributed in the contract to Hyperagents; Hyperagents' report.py compares an agent-produced prediction field and excludes empty predictions from accuracy, whereas locally every sampled paper counts.
Corrected after this review: The local question adds an instruction and answer format around the paper text (disclosed for the IMO task only).

source_associations.locator: Section 4.2 Domains (Olympiad-level math grading); Appendix C.4; Section 5.3; Appendix D.1 Table 3
source_associations.finding: HyperAgents uses IMO-GradingBench (Luong et al., 2025) as a held-out meta-evaluation domain: given problem, candidate solution, reference solutions and grading guidelines, the agent predicts a discrete grade from {0, 1, 6, 7} and is scored by accuracy against expert grades on 100-task random splits. The local task reuses IMO-GradingBench and Hyperagents' subset script, scores label accuracy on a 30-item sample of the test subset, and replaces the evolved graders with a free-form solve program.

findings: Benchmark: IMO-GradingBench with accuracy against expert human grades is exactly what the paper evaluates in this domain. The filtering to points 0/1/6/7, the 300-row sample and the stratified 100-item splits come from Hyperagents' curate_subsets.py, not from the paper (which only says the splits are randomly sampled with 100 tasks each); identity with the authors' split is not verified (disclosed).

Output format: Appendix C.4 says the agent's output is a single numeric grade from {0, 1, 6, 7}. The local rule requires the word label (correct/almost/partial/incorrect) and a numeric answer such as '7' scores 0. Hyperagents' code at the pinned commit uses GROUND_TRUTH_KEY = "Reward" (the text-label column), so the local rule follows the code, but the conflict with the paper's description is not disclosed.

Sample size: 30 of the 100 test items; the paper reports test-set scores on all 100 (DGM-H 0.610, DGM-H + transfer 0.640, ProofAutoGrader-initialised 0.700 vs ProofAutoGrader 0.670) and full-benchmark accuracy/MAE for ProofAutoGrader vs BetterGrader (0.561 -> 0.601; MAE 0.178 -> 0.175). Sample size disclosed; no paper number is claimed or reproduced.
Model: the paper's grading evaluations use o4-mini at temperature 1.0 (Appendix D.1); the local default is google/gemini-2.5-flash at temperature 0. The paper's model is not named in the notes.

Candidate and role: in the paper this domain is a held-out meta-evaluation of transferred self-improvement (DGM-H + transfer for 200 iterations, optionally initialised from ProofAutoGrader). Locally a free-form solve(question, llm) program is scored directly; the candidate replacement is disclosed, the meta-evaluation role is not mentioned (minor).

Inputs: the local question adds one instruction with paraphrased grade definitions (disclosed). normalized_mae is a local diagnostic (unparsable answers count as error 7); the headline score is accuracy as in the paper.

Answer extraction ('Answer:' / \boxed{} / last line) is the suite's generic rule, although the contract labels it "Hyperagents' check"; Hyperagents' report.py compares an agent-produced prediction field (strip + lower-case).

source_associations.finding: Mind Evolution evaluates Natural Plan Meeting Planning, splitting the 1,000 tasks into the first 50 (validation) and last 50 (test) per number of friends, and reports Success Rate (Natural Plan's Solve Rate): 83.8% test with Gemini 1.5 Flash, 98.2% two-stage with Pro. The local task uses the same 500-problem test split and Natural Plan's official success criterion on a 30-problem sample, with a free-form solve program instead of evolutionary search.

findings: Benchmark and split: Natural Plan Meeting Planning with the paper's split (Appendix B: first 50 per difficulty level validation, last 50 test). The local test file holds 500 problems, 50 for each number of people 1-10 (ids 50-999), consistent with the paper.

Metric: the paper's Success Rate is Natural Plan's Solve Rate; the local checker is a port of evaluate_meeting_planning.py (meeting count before the first invalid step must equal the golden plan's). The paper searches with its own JSON-format evaluation function and does not spell out how final JSON plans are scored with Natural Plan's text-based criterion; the notes' statement that it 'reports Natural Plan's success criterion' rests on the Metrics paragraph naming Solve Rate.
Sample: a fixed 30-problem sample of the 500 test problems; the paper reports all 500 (Mind Evolution 419/500 = 83.8%, two-stage 491/500 = 98.2%). Disclosed; paper numbers not reproduced (disclosed).
Model: Gemini 1.5 Flash (gemini-1.5-flash-001), with Gemini 1.5 Pro for unsolved problems in the two-stage setting; local default google/gemini-2.5-flash at temperature 0. Disclosed.

Candidate and evaluator access: in the paper all search methods (Best-of-N, Sequential-Revision+, Mind Evolution) use a programmatic evaluator over structured JSON constraints that returns scores and textual feedback, with up to 800 candidate solutions per problem. Locally solve(question, llm) receives only the Natural Plan 5-shot prompt text, with no checker, feedback or structured constraints. The replacement of the search is disclosed; the absence of evaluator feedback is not stated.

Compute: Table 2 reports about 406 LLM calls, 5.35M input tokens and US$0.52 per problem for Mind Evolution (Flash); the local cap is USD 0.25 for the whole 30-problem evaluation (about US$0.008 per problem at gemini-2.5-flash prices), so paper-scale search is infeasible. The budget is disclosed; the gap to the paper is not.

Prompt: the paper inserts the benchmark's 5-shot examples into its own prompts (critical-thinking instructions, parent solutions); the local question is Natural Plan's prompt_5shot unchanged, which is the benchmark's input (consistent with the contract).

recreated_verified backing: validation/llm_bench-checks.json (reference_check) and the task notes cite a port-vs-official comparison of evaluate_meeting_planning.py (pinned natural-plan commit) on all 1,000 pred_5shot_pro responses shipped with Natural Plan (Gemini 1.5 Pro 5-shot outputs from the benchmark authors, not Mind Evolution outputs): 0 disagreements, accuracy 0.384 with both; all 500 golden test plans score as solved; plus unit tests in tests/test_llm_bench_plan.py. This is purely an evaluator-faithfulness check of the ported checker against the benchmark's official code; it reproduces no Mind Evolution result (no plan produced by Mind Evolution or the paper's baselines is scored, and no success rate from Table 2 is recomputed). validation/normalization-integration-checks.json only records that the seed run completed (score 0.6). The notes and protocol_description state this correctly ('only the checker was verified' / label does not establish reproduction).
Local checker deviation (KeyError/IndexError end the simulation instead of crashing) is disclosed.

source_associations.locator: Section 4 Experiments and Results; Table 1; Section 3 Eq. (1)-(2)
source_associations.finding: SICA includes 50 random LiveCodeBench questions in the benchmark set of its 15-iteration self-improvement run and reports per-iteration LCB 'benchmark accuracy' in Table 1 (0.65 at iteration 0, 0.54-0.71 across iterations); agent selection uses a utility that also weighs cost and time. The local task scores a free-form solve program on 20 of the 50 problems selected by SICA's released loader, using the code's fraction-of-tests score.

findings: Benchmark: the paper names LiveCodeBench with 50 random questions but gives no release, platform restriction, seed or selection procedure. The local selection (release_v5, functional-test LeetCode problems only, random.seed(2), first 50 kept) is taken from SICA's code at the pinned commit (whose default subset_size is 8); the notes disclose this, but do not say that identity with the 50 questions used in the paper's run is unverifiable from the paper. The restriction to functional LeetCode problems is not stated in the paper ('50 random questions from LiveCodeBench').

Metric: locally each problem scores the fraction of its public and private tests passed, averaged over problems. SICA's score_problem at the pinned commit does compute passed/total (checked), so this follows the code; the paper only calls the LCB number 'Benchmark Accuracy' without defining it, and it differs from LiveCodeBench's standard pass@1 (all tests must pass). The contract states the fraction metric but not that it differs from standard LiveCodeBench scoring (minor).

Private tests: SICA's loader silently drops private tests for 20 of the 50 problems; the local default uses all tests (stricter), with private_tests='sica_loader' reproducing SICA (disclosed). Paper numbers are therefore not directly comparable even for identical solutions.
Sample: a fixed 20-problem sample of the 50; the paper evaluates all 50 at each iteration (disclosed).
Utility: the paper selects agents with U = 0.5*score + 0.25*cost + 0.25*time ($10 cost cap, 300 s timeout, 0.5 timeout penalty); locally only the benchmark score is used (disclosed).
Execution: SICA runs each test in Docker with 20 s per test (from the code, not the paper); locally 20 s per test and 60 s per problem in a resource-limited child process (disclosed).

Model and compute: the paper runs the agent with Sonnet 3.5 (v2) plus an o3-mini reasoning agent, with average per-problem costs of about $1.6-2.7 across its benchmarks (Table 1); locally google/gemini-2.5-flash with USD 0.25 for the whole 20-problem evaluation. The local model is disclosed; the paper's models and the cost gap are not.

Contamination: the 50 problems date from 2023-05 to 2025-01; LiveCodeBench's premise is evaluating on problems released after a model's cutoff, which the default 2025 model does not satisfy for most of them (not discussed; minor for a local optimization task).
Problem statement: the contract says 'SICA's layout', but llm_bench_lcb.statement words the prompt locally (its docstring says 'worded locally'); minor.

recreated_verified backing: validation/llm_bench-checks.json and the notes cite (1) SICA's from_raw run on the full release_v5 files with random.seed(2) selecting exactly the 50 locked problems, (2) per-test verdict agreement with SICA's generated test files for 3 correct and 1 wrong solution over 125 tests, (3) the documented private-test drop. These are data-selection and evaluator-faithfulness checks against SICA's code (small parity sample of 4 solutions); none concerns the paper's results, and no Table 1 value is reproduced. validation/normalization-integration-checks.json only records that the seed run completed (score 0.857).

source_associations.locator: Section IV-A Dataset, Table I; Section IV-D Performance Indicators; Table II
source_associations.finding: CoCoEvo introduces and evaluates the LeetCode-Contest dataset (80 weekly/biweekly contest problems released after March 2024, about 644 ground-truth tests each, examples removed) with pass@1, where a single submitted program must pass all ground-truth tests. The local task reuses that dataset (80 problems, 51,552 tests, the 20 contests of Table I) and the all-tests pass@1 rule on a 20-problem sample, with a free-form solve program instead of CoCoEvo's co-evolution.

findings: Benchmark: LeetCode-Contest as defined in Section IV-A/Table I. The local data matches the paper: 80 problems, 51,552 tests (= 80 x 644.40), 4 problems from each of the 20 contests listed in Table I (weekly 389-402, biweekly 127-132), prompts with examples removed. The paper itself does not link the Hugging Face dataset or code; the association rests on these matching counts and the authors' repository. The 20/39/21 difficulty split is not in the paper.

Metric: pass@1 with 'correct = passes all ground-truth tests' matches Section IV-D. The paper averages 5 random repeats of tie-breaking selection; locally one deterministic submission per problem is scored (minor).
Sample: fixed 20-problem sample of the 80; the paper reports all 80 (Table II, e.g. CoCoEvo 49.75 / 55.75 / 45.00 / 76.25 for the four models). Disclosed; not reproduced (disclosed).

Model and budget: the paper uses GPT-4o-mini, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, Llama-3.1-70B and DeepSeek-V3 with 100 code-generation calls and 10 test-generation calls (up to 10 tests each) per problem; locally google/gemini-2.5-flash at temperature 0 with USD 0.25 per 20-problem evaluation. The local model is disclosed; the paper's models and call budget are not named.

Leakage: the paper selects problems released after March 2024 so that its models are unlikely to have seen them; the local default model (gemini-2.5-flash, 2025) postdates these problems, so that protection does not carry over (not disclosed).
Execution: CoCoEvo's 2 s / five-process assert runner comes from the code, not the paper; locally 10 s per problem and plain-data comparison (objects with custom __eq__ fail). Disclosed.

recreated_verified backing: validation/llm_bench-checks.json and the notes cite that all 80 official solutions pass all 51,552 tests in the local harness (4.8 s), every test parsing as entry_point(args) == literal, plus unit tests (wrong/crashing code, forged __eq__). This is an evaluator sanity check (no false negatives on reference solutions); it is not a parity check against CoCoEvo's code_evaluator on incorrect programs and reproduces no Table II value. validation/normalization-integration-checks.json only records the completed seed run (score 0.55).

source_associations.finding: GEPA uses IFBench as its instruction-following benchmark. It optimizes a 2-stage system (answer first, then rewrite to satisfy the constraints) on train/validation splits (150/300) drawn from IF-RLVR Train, and tests on 294 IFBench prompts with Qwen3 8B and GPT-4.1 Mini (Tables 1-2, Appendix E.1). The local task scores a 30-prompt sample of the same 294-prompt test set. It uses a free-form candidate and the metric from the artifact, and the notes disclose both.

source_associations.locator: Section 5.1 Setup ('Tasks.', 'Models.', 'Reporting protocol.'); Table 2; Section 3 'Data pools.'; Appendix C Reproducibility, Table 8
source_associations.finding: Pairwise Validator evolves IFBench prompts with GEPA as the engine: 200 iterations, a 30-example validation pool and a 30-example test pool from its own three-way partition, five open-weight agents, and test score at the best-validation checkpoint reported as 'Accuracy (%)' (Section 5.1, Table 2, Table 8). The association is unverified because the task's locator 'Section 5, Table 1 task inventory' is wrong (Table 1 is the method-flavor table). The paper also never says its 30-item test pool comes from GEPA's 294-prompt test set, and its full-reward GEPA score for Qwen3-8B (78.3) cannot be compared with GEPA's 38.61. Its locator was corrected to Section 5.1 (Tasks), Table 2 and Appendix C (Table 8), so the association holds at the benchmark level.

findings: Data: GEPA reports results on all 294 IFBench test prompts (Appendix E.1). The local task scores a fixed seeded sample of 30 of those prompts (disclosed); the local file holds 294 prompts.

Candidate: GEPA optimizes the instructions of a fixed 2-stage DSPy program, using 150 training and 300 validation examples split from IF-RLVR Train, and never shows the test constraints to the optimizer. The local candidate is a free-form solve(question, llm) program. No train or validation data is supplied, and the candidate is scored on (and presumably optimized against) test prompts. The free-form candidate is disclosed; the change in data access is not.

Models: GEPA uses Qwen3 8B (temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k 20) and GPT-4.1 Mini (temperature 1.0), with a context window of up to 16384 tokens (Appendix E.2). The local default is google/gemini-2.5-flash at temperature 0. The client caps each call's output at 8192 tokens and the evaluation budget is USD 0.25 (model, temperature and budget are disclosed).

Metric: the GEPA paper text reports an IFBench percentage but never defines how it is computed. The local metric is the fraction of a prompt's instructions followed under the loose 8-variant rule. That metric, and the claim that the checkers are copied byte for byte, come from the pinned artifact (ifbench_metric.py) and cannot be checked against the paper. llm_bench_ifbench.py implements the 8 variants as described.
Local deviations disclosed in the notes: a checker exception counts as 'not followed' for that variant (reported as checker_errors), and NLTK and spaCy resources load offline from hash-locked data.

Scores are not comparable with GEPA's Table 1/2 IFBench numbers (Qwen3 8B: baseline 36.90, GEPA 38.61; GPT-4.1 Mini: baseline 47.79, GEPA 52.72) because the model, sample and candidate interface differ. No reproduction was attempted (disclosed).

Second paper (Pairwise Validator): IFBench is one of six GEPA-evolved tasks (Section 5.1). The validation pool has 30 examples and the test pool 30 (Table 8, 'deliberately smaller' low-data regime), with 200 iterations, the agents Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-8B (thinking), Qwen3-32B, Gemma-4 and gpt-oss-20b, and results reported as 'Accuracy (%)' at the best-validation checkpoint (Table 2). The task's PV locator is wrong, so this association is unverified. The task-level verdict rests only on the GEPA association.

The only disclosure of the Pairwise Validator differences is the README's generic merged-route paragraph: sharing a local evaluator does not establish identical paper experiments, datasets or candidate contracts.

Splits are 111/111/221 train/validation/test (Appendix E.1, Tables 1-2). The local task samples 20 of the 221 test items and scores them with a judge-based re-implementation of the artifact's metric (disclosed).

The association is unverified because the task's locator 'Section 5, Table 1 task inventory' is wrong (Table 1 is the method-flavor table). findings: Data: GEPA tests on 221 PUPA items (Appendix E.1). The local file has 221 items (ids 222-442 of PUPA pupa_new, the artifact's test rows), and each evaluation uses a fixed 20-item sample (disclosed). The candidate sees only the user query (disclosed).

Metric: the paper says only that the aggregate score consists of a response quality score and a PII leakage score. The formula (quality + 1 - leakage)/2, quality judged in both orders, and GPT-4.1-mini as judge all come from the artifact's papillon_utils.py and cannot be checked against the paper. Local deviations are disclosed: paraphrased judge prompts, deduplicated PII units, unparsable counts treated as full leakage, and leakage judged over everything sent to the untrusted client.

Models: the paper says each compound system is instantiated once per model with all modules relying on the same model (Qwen3 8B at temperature 0.6, or GPT-4.1 Mini at 1.0). It never names an untrusted model or a judge model. The note's 'GPT-4.1-mini as the untrusted model and the judge' therefore comes from the artifact, not the paper. Locally, Qwen3-8B is the trusted model (the seed program asks it not to think) and GPT-4.1-mini is the untrusted model and judge. All three run through OpenRouter at the client's default temperature 0.
Candidate: a free-form solve(user_query, llm, untrusted_llm) replaces GEPA's optimized prompts for the fixed two-module PAPILLON program (disclosed).

Leakage scoring gap: llm_bench_pupa.judge_item sets leakage to 0 when the candidate never calls untrusted_llm. A candidate that answers with the trusted model alone therefore gets full privacy credit and is judged only on quality. In GEPA, the untrusted call is a fixed part of the PAPILLON pipeline.

Scores are not comparable with GEPA's PUPA results (Qwen3 8B: baseline 80.82, GEPA 91.85; GPT-4.1 Mini: baseline 78.57, GEPA 94.47). The judge is a model, so `valid` is null. No reproduction was attempted (disclosed).

PV calls the task 'redacting PII' and gives no metric details. The locator is wrong, so this association is unverified; the task-level verdict rests on GEPA.

findings: Data: MCE's FiNER test split has 100 instances covering 12 debt/credit tags (Appendix A.1). The local file has 100 items, and its gold tags cover exactly those 12 tags. Each evaluation uses a fixed 30-item sample (disclosed).

Metric: the paper reports pass@1 prediction accuracy. The local rule (first comma-separated element, case-insensitive, read from the 'Answer:' marker, else the last \boxed{}, else the last line) replaces MCE's JSON final_answer field (disclosed). The comparison rule itself comes from the artifact's _finer_answer_is_correct and is not described in the paper.

Locally, the candidate is a free-form solve with google/gemini-2.5-flash at temperature 0 and gets no training split (disclosed).

Prompt: the paper's generator prompt template is not used. The local question is the 139-tag US GAAP context string, the 'What is best tag for entity ... in sentence ...' question, and a request for one tag (disclosed in the contract).
Scores are not comparable with MCE Table 1 (FiNER: base 58.0, MCE 75.0 offline and 68.0 online). No reproduction was attempted (disclosed).

Problem (wrong paper number in the notes): the upgrade notes say MCE learns 'from a 200-instance training split'. For USPTO-50k the paper samples 50 training and 30 validation instances (Appendix A.2); 200/100 is the FiNER split. The local evaluator supplies no training data, so the error does not change what is scored, and the task's main claim (MCE's 100-item USPTO-50k test sample, exact-match accuracy) still holds. Metric: the paper reports 'pass@1 exact match accuracy' without defining the comparison. The local rule (set of '.'-separated SMILES components, stripped and lower-cased, no canonicalisation) comes from the artifact (disclosed). Lower-casing conflates aromatic (lower-case) and aliphatic (upper-case) atom symbols, so a chemically different reactant can count as a match. That makes the rule slightly more lenient than a literal match, and the notes do not spell this out.

Model and candidate: MCE uses DeepSeek V3.1 as the generator and learns context over five epochs (offline) or online. Locally, the candidate is a free-form solve with google/gemini-2.5-flash at temperature 0 and gets no training split (disclosed).

source_associations.finding: EvoOR-Agent evaluates the cleaned NLP4LP set (178 of 269 problems, cleaned versions of its reference [48], Xiao et al.) as a held-out out-of-distribution benchmark. It scores objective-value accuracy with relative error at most 1e-3 (Eq. 7) and reports results in Table III, with a best of 97.75% using GPT-5. The local task reuses the [48] cleaned release with the same objective-accuracy rule on a fixed 30-problem sample, with a free-form candidate and a different model.

findings: Benchmark: the paper uses 'post-cleaned versions [48]' of six benchmarks. TABLE I gives NLP4LP as 269 original and 178 cleaned, and S-II.1 says it evaluates '178 verified instances'. [48] is Xiao et al., 'A survey of optimization modeling meets llms' (arXiv:2508.10047), matching the task's second paper source.

Data identity: I checked the cleaned release LLM4OR/LLM4OR@75962df5 static/clean_benchmarks/NL4LP. It contains exactly 178 numbered problem directories, identical to the hard-coded NL4LP_IDS list in llm_bench_sources.py, and the data lock records 356 files (description.txt and solution.json for each). The count therefore matches the paper.

Further cleaning: S-II.1 says EvoOR-Agent went beyond [48] with 'further manual cross-verification and deep cleaning' and converted the data into a unified format. Its converted NLP4LP file is not in the pinned release, so the problem text and gold values may differ from the local copy even though the count is the same. The notes disclose that identity is not established but not that the paper claims additional cleaning.

Metric: the paper scores |ŷ−y| / max(|y|, ε_y) ≤ 1e-3, with ε_y 'a small constant used only to avoid division by zero'. The local rule is |ŷ−y| ≤ 1e-3·max(1, |y|). In the local data all 172 non-zero gold objectives have |y| ≥ 1, so the rules coincide there. For the 6 problems whose gold objective is exactly 0, the local rule accepts |ŷ| ≤ 1e-3 where the paper's rule requires essentially exact zero. The note's rationale ('so that zero optima remain scorable') overlooks that the paper's ε_y already handles zero; the effect is negligible.

Answer extraction: in the paper the objective comes from executing agent-generated solver code. Locally the evaluator parses the last numeric literal of the candidate's final answer text (disclosed in the contract). The question gets an appended request for the optimal objective value.

Sample and repetitions: the local score is a single evaluation on a fixed 30-of-178 sample (seed 0). The paper reports the mean ± SD over ten independent runs on all 178 problems (disclosed: 'fixed 30-problem sample', 'not comparable with the paper').

source_associations.finding: EvoOR-Agent evaluates the cleaned ReSocratic (OptiBench, its reference [22]) set as a held-out out-of-distribution benchmark (605 to 403 problems). It scores objective-value accuracy with relative error at most 1e-3 and reports results in Table III, with a best of 92.55% using DeepSeek-v3.2. The local task reuses the [48] cleaned 403-problem file but replaces objective-only accuracy with a stricter all-requested-quantities criterion, which is disclosed.

findings: Benchmark: TABLE I gives ReSocratic as 605 original and 403 cleaned, and S-II.1 says 'we selected 403 validated problems'. The paper's 'ReSocratic' [22] is the OptiBench evaluation set (Yang et al.), which the task correctly calls 'OptiBench/ReSocratic'.

Data identity: I confirmed the local file is LLM4OR/LLM4OR@75962df5 static/clean_benchmarks/ReSocratic.jsonl (337,356 bytes in both the GitHub listing and the data lock). The derived resocratic.json has 403 problems, matching the paper's count. S-II.1 says EvoOR-Agent did further manual cleaning beyond [48] and converted the data into a unified format. Its converted file is not in the pinned release, so text and gold identity is unverified. The notes disclose the missing file but not the paper's claim of further cleaning.

Metric (main difference): the paper counts a problem correct if the generated objective value is within relative error 1e-3 (Eq. 7). Locally every requested quantity (objective and any requested decision variables) must match within max(1e-4, 1e-3·|gold|). I confirmed that 394 of the 403 local problems request more than one quantity. The local score is therefore stricter and can reject alternative optimal solutions. This is disclosed in the notes and contract.

Tolerance provenance: the notes call the all-quantities rule 'OptiBench's per-problem criterion'. That is correct for requiring every quantity: in yangzhch6/ReSocratic@27ff7ecb gpt_baseline.py, line_correct requires each key to match. OptiBench's tolerance, however, is an absolute abs(llm_ans - gt_ans) < 1e-4 on answers rounded to 5 decimals. The local max(1e-4, 1e-3·|gold|) is a hybrid that is neither OptiBench's nor EvoOR-Agent's rule. The local tolerance itself is stated in the contract.

Answer format: OptiBench asks for each quantity in separate follow-up turns after running code, and EvoOR-Agent extracts the objective from executed solver code. Locally the candidate returns one JSON object of all quantities (disclosed).
Sample and repetitions: one evaluation on a fixed 30-of-403 sample (seed 0), against the paper's mean over ten runs on all 403 (disclosed).

Candidate and model: a free-form solve(question, llm) program with google/gemini-2.5-flash at temperature 0, against the paper's evolved AOE workflow with DeepSeek-v3.2, GPT-5, Gemini 3 Flash or Qwen 3Max (disclosed).

Train/test role: the paper never shows ReSocratic to the evolutionary search; it is reserved for out-of-distribution evaluation. Locally the program search is scored directly on the same fixed 30 ReSocratic items. The ReSocratic notes do not mention the held-out role at all.

Paper number: Table III and Section IV-B report EvoOR-Agent's best ReSocratic accuracy as 92.55% (DeepSeek-v3.2). It is not embedded (labels.reference = 'none'), which is consistent, and it would not be comparable anyway because of the stricter metric.

source_associations.locator: Section 3.1 (Function Inlining for Size): Figure 2 (Evolvable blocks for function inlining), the two settings (a) Partial Heuristics / (b) Full Heuristics, Figure 3 (Evolutionary curve of binary size reduction on internal search benchmark) and the 4.27% / 5.23% results; evolved API-level policy printed in Appendix A (Magellan-Generated Inlining Policy for Binary Size)
source_associations.finding: Section 3.1 evaluates evolved LLVM inlining policies for binary size: a feature-based setting composing 38 MLInlineAdvisor features inside MLModelRunner::evaluateUntyped (4.27%) and an API-level setting in MLInlineAdvisor::getAdviceImpl (5.23%), rewarded by the final linked binary size of Google's internal search application relative to LLVM's upstream heuristic, starting from an always-false policy. The task is a disclosed proxy of the feature-based setting (Python policy over LLVM 23's 38 MLInlineAdvisor features via the interactive ML-inliner channel, SQLite sqlite3 shell, text-section bytes / default heuristic), so it supports the benchmark/objective claim but its notes misdescribe two paper details.

findings: Workload: the paper searches on an internal search application (and reports temporal generalization on four monthly snapshots and domain generalization on more than ten internal production binaries); the task builds the public SQLite 3.53.4 sqlite3 shell (two translation units, sqlite3.c and shell.c). Disclosed.

Toolchain: the paper runs on Google's internal clang/LLVM toolchain tracking tip-of-tree (summer 2025 commits); the task uses any LLVM >= 17 with the interactive ML inliner (reference run Homebrew LLVM 23.1.1, arm64 macOS). The notes disclose that sizes and the feature set depend on LLVM version and target, but do not say the paper used an internal, non-release toolchain.

Build pipeline: the task compiles with clang -Oz -Xclang -disable-llvm-optzns, runs opt -passes=default<O2>, llc -O2 and links with clang, without (Thin)LTO; the paper does not give the flags of its search build (its domain-generalization study uses 'production optimization flags'). I confirmed locally (opt --version only on a trivial module) that Homebrew LLVM 23.1.1 opt rejects default<Oz> ('no longer supported. Use O2 in conjunction with the minsize attribute instead'), as the notes say.

Metric: the paper reports percent size reduction of the final linked binary versus LLVM's upstream heuristic (measured e.g. via llvm-size; it does not say whether whole-file size or a section size). The task scores text-section bytes (__text/.text from llvm-size -A) of the linked binary divided by the same build with the default heuristic (minimize; reduction = 1 - score), which excludes data, constant and unwind sections. The text-section choice is stated in the notes and contract.

Policy interface: the paper's feature-based policies are C++ code compiled into LLVM (AERunner::evaluateUntyped), with tunable constants exposed as compiler flags and optionally tuned by Vizier; the task's policy is a Python should_inline(features) answering LLVM's InteractiveModelRunner pipes (itself an MLModelRunner), with no flag/autotuner layer. The paper's API-level setting (its best result, 5.23%, and the Appendix A policy) cannot be expressed through the feature-only interface. Disclosed.

Features: the paper composes 38 predefined features from InlineModelFeatureMaps.h at llvm-project commit c878baf1; the task exposes the 38 features of LLVM 23 (same count; names and semantics are version dependent, which the notes disclose).
Legality and mandatory inlining stay with LLVM's MLInlineAdvisor in both the paper and the task; the always-false seed matches the paper's starting point ('a naive policy that always returns false').

Search: the paper uses AlphaEvolve with Gemini-2.5-Pro for 1.5 days of sequential exploration (plus a Vizier-augmented variant reaching >5% in about 5 hours); the task fixes no search method, model or budget.

Reported numbers (4.27%, 5.23%, >5% with autotuning, 5.75-5.95% temporal, 8.79% domain average) are on the internal application and are not comparable with the local ratio; the notes quote 4.27% and 5.23% only as context.

PROBLEM (note inaccuracy): the upgrade notes say 'Magellan plugs evolved C++ heuristics into MLInlineAdvisor::getAdviceImpl, either composing the MLInlineAdvisor features (4.27%) or calling LLVM APIs directly (5.23%)'. The paper (Section 3.1, Figure 2) places the feature-based setting in MLModelRunner::evaluateUntyped (AERunner) and only the full/API-level setting in getAdviceImpl (AEInlineAdvisor). The task's interactive model runner is therefore closer to the paper's partial-heuristic hook than the notes state.

PROBLEM (note inaccuracy): the notes say 'Magellan's evolved heuristics are not released'. Appendix A prints the evolved API-level binary-size policy (AEInlineAdvisor::getAdviceImpl, described in Section 3.1.3 as 143 lines) and Appendix B the performance policy; only the feature-based (4.27%) policy is not printed.

Metadata: task.json still carries pre-upgrade text (evaluation.protocol 'specified_only', validation.level 'paper_inventory', the generic limitations, and execution.notes 'Search workloads and/or private contest test instances are not public...'); the upgrade notes appear only in problem.json and README.md. task.json/problem.json 'requires' omit bin:clang although the contract and module need clang.

Locator: task.json 'Sections 3.1-3.3' contains the relevant Section 3.1 but also Section 3.2 (inlining for performance) and 3.3 (register allocation and XLA); a narrower locator ('Section 3.1, Figures 2-3, Appendix A') is suggested. Not a mismatch.

source_associations.finding: Section 3.3 evaluates XLA auto-sharding as the ASPLOS'25 IOPDDL contest problem (one strategy per node, minimise node plus resharding cost under a time-varying memory limit), searching on the 5 public instances and evaluating on the 20 private ones with the contest's objective and scoring, and reports only 'comparable to top contest submissions'. The task reuses the contest problem, a port of the official cost evaluator and the contest's best-team normalisation, but scores the 5 public (search) instances with a 10 s Python budget; these differences are disclosed.

findings: Instances: the task scores A, G, M, S, Y, the five public instances that the paper used for search/training; the paper evaluates on the 20 instances withheld during the contest. All 25 instances (A-Y) are in benchmarks/ of google/iopddl at the pinned commit 8a61c4359c5a330a04c8ef1780402cc254d28f29 (checked the directory listing), and IOPDDL.md states all benchmarks become public after the contest, so the paper's evaluation split is available but unused. The notes disclose that the 20 are not used; the consequence is that the local score is measured on the paper's search set (no held-out evaluation).
Aggregation: mean contest points over 5 instances versus the contest's sum of points over its 20 evaluation instances. Disclosed.

Normalisation: points = fixed best submitted team cost (minimum over teams in misc/iopddl_final_results.csv @0626750) / candidate cost, so a candidate that beats every team can exceed 1 point; in the contest the minimum includes the scored team itself, capping points at 1. Implied by the notes, not stated.

Time budget: solve() gets 10 s wall clock in the evaluator process (+1 s grace) versus per-benchmark limits of 1 to 5 minutes, generously enforced, on a dedicated 8-core, 32 GB Linux workstation (IOPDDL.md). Disclosed; the notes' wording 'C++ binaries' is loose, IOPDDL.md only requires a binary executable named iopddl (the starter code is C++).

Infeasible/empty/late answers: the task gives 0 points and the notes call this 'the contest's treatment of missing solutions'. IOPDDL.md (fetched at the pinned asplos-contest commit) allows an empty list [] when no solution is found but does not state how empty, infeasible or late answers are scored; I could not verify this attribution (it may come from the final-results CSV, which I did not inspect).

Interface: Python solve(problem dict, time_limit_s) instead of a binary reading a JSON path and timeout; wrong-length, non-integer or out-of-range answers make the whole candidate invalid rather than scoring 0 on one benchmark.

Paper metric: the paper adopts 'the same objective and scoring function as the competition' but gives no numeric Magellan score, so there is no paper number to compare with; the reference values used are the contest's published team costs.

Starting point and search: the paper feeds IOPDDL.md to Gemini-2.5-Pro for the initial solution and evolves for one week; the local seed is a greedy plus best-response heuristic. The notes say Magellan's 'search budget' is not released, but the paper states 'one week of evolution' (minor inaccuracy).

Framing: the paper notes the instances derive from real models (diffusion, Gemma) and that integration into the full XLA pipeline is still in progress; neither the paper's experiment nor the task runs XLA, consistent with the task name following the paper's 'auto-sharding in XLA' framing.

Metadata: task.json execution.notes and source_specification.execution_notes still say 'Search workloads and/or private contest test instances are not public', contradicted by the pinned repository (all 25 instances) and by the task's own note that the 20 were 'published afterwards'; evaluation.protocol 'specified_only', validation.level 'paper_inventory' and the generic limitations are pre-upgrade text.

source_associations.finding: Section 3.3 evaluates evolved extraction heuristics for e-graphs produced by Enzyme-JAX equality saturation of XLA programs, minimising the total cost of the extracted program under a per-e-node cost model, and reports a 7% improvement over manually designed policies. The task keeps the problem (valid acyclic extraction from root e-classes, minimise summed e-node cost) but runs on public Tensat e-graphs from extraction-gym with their costs and normalises by extraction-gym's faster-greedy-dag extractor; it is labelled a proxy in its notes.

findings: Data: five Tensat (TASO rewrite rules) e-graphs of VGG, ResNet-50, BERT, NASNet-A and NASRNN from extraction-gym @903ba0f instead of the paper's Enzyme-JAX (XLA) e-graphs, which are not public. Disclosed ('Clearly labelled proxy').
Cost model: per-e-node costs stored in the Tensat files instead of the paper's (unspecified) Enzyme-JAX cost model. Disclosed.

Objective: the paper minimises 'the total cost of the extracted program' without saying whether shared e-classes are counted once (DAG cost) or per use (tree cost); the task uses extraction-gym's DAG cost. The paper's validity definition (one e-node per reachable e-class from designated roots, children's e-classes selected, no cycles) matches the task's check_extraction.

Baseline and score: the paper's 7% is relative to unnamed 'manually designed policies'; the task scores the geometric mean over five e-graphs of candidate DAG cost / precomputed faster-greedy-dag DAG cost (minimise). Not comparable with the paper's 7%; disclosed ('Scores are not comparable with Magellan's results').
Headroom: optimal (ILP) costs were not computed, so the distance to optimum is unknown. Disclosed.
Budget: 30 s wall clock per extract call in the evaluator process; the paper gives no budget. Disclosed.

Not verified by me: the reference and bottom-up DAG costs in params (from a local extraction-gym run), the claim that the unpruned Tensat files contain cycles, and the bit-for-bit port checks (no evaluator was run).

Zenodo claim: record 16916484 is the artifact of 'Mind the Abstraction Gap: Bringing Equality Saturation to Real-World ML Compilers' (Vohra et al., cited by Magellan as the Enzyme-JAX eqsat work) and holds a single 15.2 kB zip linked to a GitHub software repository, consistent with 'code only'; the zip contents were not inspected.

Presentation: the task name, description, benchmark and source_specification still read 'XLA/Enzyme-JAX e-graph extraction task evaluated in Magellan', and the contract does not mention Tensat; the proxy status is disclosed only in the notes (problem.json, README.md) and the extraction-gym source locator. task.json limitations, execution.notes ('private contest test instances are not public', irrelevant here), evaluation.protocol 'specified_only' and validation.level 'paper_inventory' are pre-upgrade.
Locator: task.json 'Sections 3.1-3.3' contains the relevant Section 3.3, but 3.1-3.2 concern LLVM inlining; 'Section 3.3 (Preliminary Results on Other Problems)' is suggested. Not a mismatch.

The task runs the unchanged Frontier-CS checker on the 70 official inputs of problem 0 with a local judge harness and the judge's mean-ratio x 100 score; harness differences are disclosed, but comparability with the paper's numbers is not discussed.

findings: Benchmark identity: the paper names only 'the Polyominoes packing problem from Frontier-CS' (no problem id or variant); the mapping to Frontier-CS algorithmic problem 0 'Pack the Polyominoes (Reflections Allowed)' comes from CORAL's examples/frontier_cs_algo/0 (pinned task.yaml: problem_id 0, 70 cases, 2 s, 256 MB, C++17), which is cited as a source.

Test data: 70 inputs and the unchanged chk.cc from Frontier-CS @e6ef46e. CORAL's grader called the Frontier-CS judge (go-judge in Docker) via an unpinned frontier_cs install. Per the GitHub history of algorithmic/problems/0/testdata (fetched), the data were added 2025-12-14, reduced to a single case on 2026-07-08 (#160) and restored on 2026-07-26 (#171); the paper's arXiv v1 dates from April 2026, so its runs presumably used the December 2025 set. The notes say only 'testdata last changed 2026-07-25'; that the restored files equal the set used in the paper's runs was not verified.

Harness: local GNU g++ -O2 -pipe -std=gnu++17 without -static -s; setrlimit launcher with 2 s CPU / 4 s wall; memory as address-space limit on Linux but only post-hoc peak RSS on macOS; stack capped by the OS; four cases in parallel. Disclosed.

Metric: the paper reports a 'score'/'coverage' percentage without defining the aggregation over test cases; the task uses the Frontier-CS judge-engine rule (mean over cases of the checker's total cells / (W x H) on accepted outputs, x 100, 0 for rejected/failed cases), consistent with 'coverage'.

source_associations.finding: The paper evaluates LLM-generated CPMpy reformulations of car sequencing (CSPLib problem 1), one of its eight CSPLib satisfaction problems, by baseline-relative PAR2 runtime speedup on single-worker CP-SAT. 29 of 30 runs beat the baseline (per-problem GM 3.1x; best 5.8x). The local task keeps this objective and candidate interface but uses its own instances, baseline and CPU-time measure, all disclosed.

findings: The paper evaluates car sequencing (CSPLib problem 1) explicitly. 29 of 30 runs beat the baseline, with per-problem GM 3.1x over all strategies (Section 6.1). The best model reaches 5.8x (Full-history) using a Boolean class-position viewpoint and option-profile aggregation (Table 3). The PDR GM is 3.33 (Table 5).

Local instances: five options with the classic CSPLib capacities 1/2, 2/3, 1/3, 2/5 and 1/5. Classes and demands come from a planted random window-respecting sequence of 40-100 cars from a pool of 12 random option sets plus the empty set. The paper does not describe the sizes of its AutoIG car-sequencing instances. Disclosed.
The local baseline (Count per class plus element-indexed window sums) is a local Essence translation. The paper's car-sequencing baseline is not available for comparison.

Instances: the paper uses AutoIG-generated pools from streamliner research (Spracklen et al. 2023), remeasures them with its CPMpy/OR-Tools baseline, keeps satisfiable instances with baseline runtime in [1,300] s, bins them into eight equal-frequency runtime bins and samples an 8/8/16 train/validation/test split. The local task uses 8 locally generated or hand-selected satisfiable instances, graded so that the local baseline takes about 0.1-6 CPU s. Disclosed in the notes.

Split and selection: the paper searches on 8 training instances, selects the final model on 8 validation instances (baseline as fallback) and reports speedups on 16 held-out test instances, as a GM over 3 repetitions x 10 strategies (Tables 2, 4 and 5). The local task scores a single fixed, visible set of 8 instances with no held-out set. Disclosed (overfitting note).

Baseline: the paper pairs each problem with a 'parameterised baseline model' that is not released; only the covering-array baseline is printed (Appendix D, Listing 7). The local baseline is a CPMpy translation of the CSPLib Essence model written for this package, so the local reference runtime differs from the paper's. Disclosed.

Time measure: the local runtime is the CPU seconds of build_model + CPMpy-to-OR-Tools transformation + CP-SAT Solve (separate worker process) + extractor. The paper defines tau(m,d) as 'solving time' and says it measures 'the time to first solution'. It does not say whether this is wall-clock or CPU time, or whether model construction and CPMpy transformation are counted. The notes' statement that 'The paper reports solving time on wall clock' is not supported by the paper text.

Solver configuration matches the paper: CPMpy 0.10.1, OR-Tools CP-SAT with one search worker (Section 5) and seed 42 (Appendix A). The paper does not give its OR-Tools version; the local version is 9.14.6206.

Caps and PAR2: the local per-instance cap is max(1 s, 3 x baseline CPU s) and a timeout counts 2 x cap, so a timeout costs at most 6x the baseline time. The paper uses a fixed 300 s per-instance limit, so a timeout counts 600 s at validation and test (Appendix B). During search the paper also bounds each candidate's total training evaluation with C_B = max(T_B, min(1.5 T_B, 900)) s (Section 5 'Configurations.'). The notes disclose the 300 s limit but do not mention the C_B rule. Instances on which the local baseline does not finish within 60 s are dropped, and the evaluation fails if more than half are dropped. The paper excludes an instance when its live baseline times out. The whole local evaluation is limited to 240 s.

Score: the local score is sum(baseline s) / sum(candidate s) over the 8 instances. This matches the paper's per-run speedup T_S(B)/T_S(m) with PAR2 (Section 5 'Instances and Measures.'). The paper's reported numbers aggregate many such speedups by geometric mean across runs, so they are not comparable with a local score. No paper number is stated in the task.

Validity: the paper accepts an answer when fixing it into the baseline model leaves the baseline satisfiable (Section 3, Definition 1). Locally an independent checker of the CSPLib definition verifies each answer. Disclosed. Rejecting infeasibility claims and objectives fits the paper's satisfaction setting and its false-UNSAT accounting.

Candidate interface matches the paper's prompt rules (Appendix A, Listing 1): build_model(data) -> (model, extractor), the same input and answer structure as the baseline, and cpmpy, numpy and the standard library. The local import allowlist is a stricter subset of the standard library. Disclosed.

The paper's object of study is the LLM search procedure: DeepSeek V4 Flash, 100 iterations, ten strategies, 3 repetitions. The local task isolates the per-problem reformulation objective that this procedure optimises. The SCiEL config shipped with the task (gemini-2.5-flash, OpenEvolve islands) is unrelated to the paper's search setup.
Hardware: the paper ran on an Intel Core i7-12700 with up to 8 concurrent single-core runs. The local instances were graded on an Apple M-series CPU and evaluated sequentially.

Metadata: task.json still has kind 'specification', evaluation.protocol 'specified_only', validation.level 'paper_inventory', benchmark 'CSPLib / AutoIG' and requirements.notes 'AutoIG instance pools'. The local recreated evaluator uses no AutoIG instances, and the task.json limitations do not repeat the protocol differences, which appear only in problem.json notes and the README.

findings: The paper evaluates BIBD (CSPLib problem 28) explicitly. Only 2 of 30 runs improve (best 1.2x), 76% of candidate evaluations time out on single training instances, and only 19 of 3,000 proposals are solution-valid (Section 6.1 'Failures.'). The paper attributes this to very wide incidence matrices such as 8 x 2744.

Local instances: 8 admissible (v, b, r, k, lambda) designs that exist, with v <= 31 and b <= 90 (the widest are 8x56, 7x70 and 10x90). These are much smaller than the paper's AutoIG BIBD instances, so the regime in which the paper's candidates failed is not represented. Disclosed in the BIBD note.
The local baseline is a Boolean incidence matrix with row, column and pairwise scalar-product sums, and no lexicographic symmetry breaking. The paper's baseline is not released.

The generic note says instances come from 'deterministic SplitMix64 streams in or_csp_csplib.py'. For this problem the generator only passes through a fixed parameter tuple with no randomness, as the problem-specific note says. This is an internal wording inconsistency, not a paper difference.

Instances: the paper uses AutoIG-generated pools from streamliner research (Spracklen et al. 2023), remeasures them with its CPMpy/OR-Tools baseline, keeps satisfiable instances with baseline runtime in [1,300] s, bins them into eight equal-frequency runtime bins and samples an 8/8/16 train/validation/test split. The local task uses 8 locally generated or hand-selected satisfiable instances, graded so that the local baseline takes about 0.1-6 CPU s. Disclosed in the notes.

Split and selection: the paper searches on 8 training instances, selects the final model on 8 validation instances (baseline as fallback) and reports speedups on 16 held-out test instances, as a GM over 3 repetitions x 10 strategies (Tables 2, 4 and 5). The local task scores a single fixed, visible set of 8 instances with no held-out set. Disclosed (overfitting note).

Baseline: the paper pairs each problem with a 'parameterised baseline model' that is not released; only the covering-array baseline is printed (Appendix D, Listing 7). The local baseline is a CPMpy translation of the CSPLib Essence model written for this package, so the local reference runtime differs from the paper's. Disclosed.

Time measure: the local runtime is the CPU seconds of build_model + CPMpy-to-OR-Tools transformation + CP-SAT Solve (separate worker process) + extractor. The paper defines tau(m,d) as 'solving time' and says it measures 'the time to first solution'. It does not say whether this is wall-clock or CPU time, or whether model construction and CPMpy transformation are counted. The notes' statement that 'The paper reports solving time on wall clock' is not supported by the paper text.

Solver configuration matches the paper: CPMpy 0.10.1, OR-Tools CP-SAT with one search worker (Section 5) and seed 42 (Appendix A). The paper does not give its OR-Tools version; the local version is 9.14.6206.

Caps and PAR2: the local per-instance cap is max(1 s, 3 x baseline CPU s) and a timeout counts 2 x cap, so a timeout costs at most 6x the baseline time. The paper uses a fixed 300 s per-instance limit, so a timeout counts 600 s at validation and test (Appendix B). During search the paper also bounds each candidate's total training evaluation with C_B = max(T_B, min(1.5 T_B, 900)) s (Section 5 'Configurations.'). The notes disclose the 300 s limit but do not mention the C_B rule. Instances on which the local baseline does not finish within 60 s are dropped, and the evaluation fails if more than half are dropped. The paper excludes an instance when its live baseline times out. The whole local evaluation is limited to 240 s.

The paper's reported numbers aggregate many such speedups by geometric mean across runs, so they are not comparable with a local score. No paper number is stated in the task.

Validity: the paper accepts an answer when fixing it into the baseline model leaves the baseline satisfiable (Section 3, Definition 1). Locally an independent checker of the CSPLib definition verifies each answer. Disclosed. Rejecting infeasibility claims and objectives fits the paper's satisfaction setting and its false-UNSAT accounting.

Split and selection: the paper searches on 8 training instances, selects the final model on 8 validation instances (baseline as fallback) and reports speedups on 16 held-out test instances, as a GM over 3 repetitions x 10 strategies (Tables 2, 4 and 5). The local task scores a single fixed, visible set of 8 instances with no held-out set. Disclosed (overfitting note).

Baseline: the paper pairs each problem with a 'parameterised baseline model' that is not released; only the covering-array baseline is printed (Appendix D, Listing 7). The local baseline is a CPMpy translation of the CSPLib Essence model written for this package, so the local reference runtime differs from the paper's. Disclosed.

Time measure: the local runtime is the CPU seconds of build_model + CPMpy-to-OR-Tools transformation + CP-SAT Solve (separate worker process) + extractor. The paper defines tau(m,d) as 'solving time' and says it measures 'the time to first solution'. It does not say whether this is wall-clock or CPU time, or whether model construction and CPMpy transformation are counted. The notes' statement that 'The paper reports solving time on wall clock' is not supported by the paper text.

Solver configuration matches the paper: CPMpy 0.10.1, OR-Tools CP-SAT with one search worker (Section 5) and seed 42 (Appendix A). The paper does not give its OR-Tools version; the local version is 9.14.6206.

Caps and PAR2: the local per-instance cap is max(1 s, 3 x baseline CPU s) and a timeout counts 2 x cap, so a timeout costs at most 6x the baseline time. The paper uses a fixed 300 s per-instance limit, so a timeout counts 600 s at validation and test (Appendix B). During search the paper also bounds each candidate's total training evaluation with C_B = max(T_B, min(1.5 T_B, 900)) s (Section 5 'Configurations.'). The notes disclose the 300 s limit but do not mention the C_B rule. Instances on which the local baseline does not finish within 60 s are dropped, and the evaluation fails if more than half are dropped. The paper excludes an instance when its live baseline times out. The whole local evaluation is limited to 240 s.

Score: the local score is sum(baseline s) / sum(candidate s) over the 8 instances. This matches the paper's per-run speedup T_S(B)/T_S(m) with PAR2 (Section 5 'Instances and Measures.'). The paper's reported numbers aggregate many such speedups by geometric mean across runs, so they are not comparable with a local score. No paper number is stated in the task.

Validity: the paper accepts an answer when fixing it into the baseline model leaves the baseline satisfiable (Section 3, Definition 1). Locally an independent checker of the CSPLib definition verifies each answer. Disclosed. Rejecting infeasibility claims and objectives fits the paper's satisfaction setting and its false-UNSAT accounting.

Candidate interface matches the paper's prompt rules (Appendix A, Listing 1): build_model(data) -> (model, extractor), the same input and answer structure as the baseline, and cpmpy, numpy and the standard library. The local import allowlist is a stricter subset of the standard library. Disclosed.

The paper's object of study is the LLM search procedure: DeepSeek V4 Flash, 100 iterations, ten strategies, 3 repetitions. The local task isolates the per-problem reformulation objective that this procedure optimises. The SCiEL config shipped with the task (gemini-2.5-flash, OpenEvolve islands) is unrelated to the paper's search setup.
Hardware: the paper ran on an Intel Core i7-12700 with up to 8 concurrent single-core runs. The local instances were graded on an Apple M-series CPU and evaluated sequentially.

source_associations.finding: Promptbreeder evaluates evolved task prompts on AddSub (Section 4, Appendix I.2) and reports test accuracy in Table 1 (87.8 zero-shot, 87.1 few-shot with PaLM 2-L) after splitting the dataset into equal random training and test halves. The local task scores a free-form solve(question, llm) program by accuracy on a 30-problem sample of a locally defined test half of the same public dataset, a disclosed adaptation.

findings: Benchmark and metric match: the paper names AddSub in Section 4 and Appendix I.2 and reports accuracy on the test half (Table 1). The task's paper locator 'Section 4 and Appendix I' is correct (the Table 1 caption itself refers to Section 4 and Appendix I); the split procedure is in the Table 1 caption and Appendix J.2 and the results in Table 1, which the locator does not name.

Data copy: the local file is the zero_shot_cot copy (395 problems; count confirmed from suite/_lib/data/llm_bench/addsub.json). Promptbreeder does not name its data source or the dataset size; it says only that it uses the datasets of prompt strategies such as Plan-and-Solve. That the paper used this exact copy is plausible but not verified.

Split: the paper takes a random, unpublished half for training and reports accuracy on the other half. Locally the halves come from a SHA-256 ordering of problem ids (197 test problems), so the test problems differ from the paper's (disclosed).
Sample size: one fixed 30-problem sample of the 197-problem test half, against the paper's whole test half (disclosed).
Model: google/gemini-2.5-flash at temperature 0 by default, against PaLM 2-L in the paper (disclosed).

Candidate interface: a free-form solve(question, llm) program replaces Promptbreeder's evolved two-stage prompt pair, which is applied as Inducer (question and prompt 1) then Evaluator (working and prompt 2), as in Plan-and-Solve (disclosed as 'evolved pair of task prompts').

Generation budget: Appendix J.2 caps Promptbreeder's Inducer at 30 sampled tokens and its Evaluator at 5. The local candidate may call the model freely, and the seed program allows 4096 tokens of chain-of-thought (not disclosed).

Problem description: Promptbreeder's arithmetic runs start from the problem description 'Solve the math word problem, giving your answer as an arabic numeral.' (Appendix G). The local question is the bare problem text and the seed asks for an 'Answer:' line (not disclosed; minor because the candidate controls the prompt).

Optimization signal: in the paper, fitness is accuracy on random batches of 100 training examples, and only the fittest individual is evaluated once on the test half. Locally the training half is never used: the score an optimizer maximizes is the fixed 30-problem test sample itself, so selection happens on the reported test items (not disclosed).
Answer scoring: the paper does not specify its answer extraction. The local rule (last numeric literal of the final answer, tolerance 1e-6) is stated in the contract (disclosed).

Zero-shot and few-shot: Table 1 reports zero-shot and few-shot Promptbreeder separately. The few-shot variant evolves contexts of correct workings drawn from training data. The local task does not say which setting it corresponds to and gives no training data (minor).

Metadata: task.json still has evaluation.protocol 'specified_only', kind 'specification' and limitations that predate the upgrade, while execution.suite.protocol is 'recreated'. The upgrade notes appear only in problem.json and README.md. No paper number is stated by the task, so none is wrong.
Not reproduced: Promptbreeder accuracies were not reproduced. Only the paper text and the local code and data files were inspected.
applied_corrections: Corrected after this review: The optimization signal is the reported test sample itself. The paper selects on training-half fitness (batches of 100) and evaluates only the final best individual on the test half; the local training half is unused.

Corrected after this review: The paper's problem description ('Solve the math word problem, giving your answer as an arabic numeral.') is not part of the local question text.
Corrected after this review: Whether the task corresponds to the zero-shot or the few-shot Promptbreeder setting is not stated; no training examples are available for few-shot contexts.

source_associations.finding: ProTeGi evaluates prompt optimization on its own Jailbreak detection dataset (452 multilingual, human-annotated user inputs) with test-set binary F1 (Section 3.1, 3.2, 3.4). The local task scores binary F1 on the public English jackhhao/jailbreak-classification test split: a proxy of the paper's experiment, clearly disclosed. The task's only paper locator, 'Section 4', points to Related Work, so the relationship cannot be marked verified as recorded. The locator was corrected to Section 3, where the paper describes the data, setup and results.

findings: Locator: task.json cites the paper at 'Section 4' (sources, evaluation.source_locator, source_specification). In the cited arXiv v2 Section 4 is 'Related Work'. The Jailbreak dataset and setup are in Section 3.1 (Data) and 3.2 (Setup), and the results are in Section 3.4 (Figure 3, Tables 1-3, Figure 4). This locator problem is the reason for 'unverified'; the relationship itself is supported as a disclosed proxy.

Data (proxy, disclosed): the paper's Jailbreak set (452 multilingual examples with human-annotated labels; user inputs to an LLM continuation API) is replaced by the public English jackhhao/jailbreak-classification balanced test split (262 prompts, 139 jailbreak, as counted in suite/_lib/data/llm_bench/jailbreak.json). The dataset card at the pinned revision confirms Apache-2.0, English, and jailbreak prompts from verazuo/jailbreak_llms and benign prompts from OpenOrca and GPTeacher. The disclosure appears in the problem.json notes, README, contract and the benchmark source locator ('proxy for the unreleased ProTeGi data').

Sample: the paper randomly samples 50 development and 150 test examples and averages 3 trials. Locally, one fixed 40-message sample of the 262-item proxy test split is evaluated deterministically (the 40-message sample is disclosed; the paper's 50/150 split and 3-trial averaging are not mentioned).

Metric: the paper reports test binary F1, max-pooled over the final beam. Locally it is the positive-class (jailbreak) F1 over the sample, with accuracy reported as per_item_accuracy. The notes correctly state that the pinned LMOps prompt_optimization/tasks.py computes f1_score(labels, preds, average='micro'), which equals accuracy (checked in the pinned file at commit 6f53ef4).

Prediction rule: LMOps BinaryPredictor predicts 1 when response.strip().upper().startswith('YES') on a 4-token completion (checked in the pinned predictors.py). findings: Benchmark and objective: Section 4 anchors the co-evolved code reviewer to CRAVE [50], 'a dataset of accepted/rejected pull requests'. Evaluator replacement ranks reviewers by the epsilon-best-belief lower bound (epsilon = 0.05) on anchor counts, not by raw accuracy (Section 3.5, Algorithm 1). Data: an analogue built from PatchCamelyon's 'valid' and 'test' files (Zenodo 2546921; 65,536 patches from 183 whole-slide images), not from Kaggle's files, which per the notes are PCam without duplicates (not checked by me). 8,045 exact duplicates are removed and patches are cut to their central 48 x 48 pixels instead of the full 96 x 96 (disclosed). I recounted the prepared arrays: 45,819 training crops (43.7% positive), 11,672 test crops (40.1% positive) from 39 slides.

Split and sample size: slide-disjoint seeded split; MLE-bench re-splits Kaggle's training images at random (test ratio about 0.21, no slide grouping; read in the work package's copy of MLE-bench's prepare.py), and the local training set is about a fifth of Kaggle's. Disclosed, with the statement that scores are not comparable and medal thresholds do not apply.

Metric and scoring: ROC AUC with predictions required to lie in [0, 1], as MLE-bench's grade.py with prepare_for_auroc_metric (the receipt records an exact match on the seed's predictions). The papers report only medals (LoongFlow) or medal rates over seven competitions (EurekAgent).

Candidate interface: fit_predict(train, test_inputs, time_budget_s) returns one probability per test crop from a sandboxed CPU child; both papers' agents build full pipelines that produce a submission file. Disclosed in the contract.

Budget and hardware: locally 600 s wall-clock on 4 CPU threads with 3.5 GB, no GPU or pretrained weights. EurekAgent used MLE-Bench's 24-hour single-GPU setting (Table 5: 12 rounds, 3 parallel sessions) with web tools; LoongFlow states no budget (its pinned task_config.yaml allows a 24 h executor timeout). The notes gave only the local budget; corrected.

Search feedback: the local evaluator scores every candidate on the test labels and that score is the search signal, with no validation split held back. LoongFlow's released evaluator (eval_program.py at 945c78bc) selects on out-of-fold predictions for the training data and grades the test submission only in a debug mode; EurekAgent says only that agents receive official scores from a hidden grading service. Not disclosed before; corrected in the notes.

Model and search: LoongFlow names Gemini-3.0-flash for this competition and EurekAgent uses Claude Code with GLM-5.1; the task fixes no search method or model, and the shipped config.yaml (google/gemini-2.5-flash, OpenEvolve islands) is unrelated to either paper.

Not verified by me: the grade.py parity, the seed score 0.8046 and the CNN probe's 0.865 (recorded in validation/kaggle-checks.json; no evaluator was run); the Zenodo MD5 and center_tumor_patch label checks (receipt); the competition data page's statement that Kaggle's data is PCam without duplicates.

Metadata (not a paper-relationship problem): task.json still has kind 'specification', evaluation.protocol 'specified_only' and validation.level 'paper_inventory'; requirements.notes and source_specification.requirements ('Kaggle dataset access and competition terms', 'GPU where applicable') describe the upstream setup, while the local evaluator needs neither Kaggle access nor a GPU.

source_associations.finding: LaSR searches for scaling laws that predict the BIG-bench multiple-choice grade from model and dataset hyperparameters on the 53,812 entries whose preferred metric is that grade, and compares four laws by validation MSE after fitting their constants on 43,049 training samples (Table 4). The local task rebuilds 53,812 rows from the BIG-bench records, splits them 43,049/10,763 at random, fits a candidate's at most five constants by Levenberg-Marquardt and scores the held-out MSE; the paper's split, matrix-valued constants, monotonicity regulariser and Pareto selection are not reproduced, which the notes disclose.

findings: Benchmark and data: Section 4.6 uses the BIG-bench entries whose preferred metric is the multiple-choice grade (53,812 samples); the local rows are rebuilt from the BIG-bench records at 092b196c (58,033 such entries minus 4,221 of models without a decoding temperature) and match that count. Appendix A.6 names the same three model families that remain locally (GPT, dense BIG-G, sparse BIG-G); Section 4.6 also says BIG-bench has scored responses from 55 language models, and whether the paper's 53,812 samples include the models dropped locally is not stated. Row identity with the paper's data is not established (the paper lists no rows). I recounted the prepared CSV: 53,812 rows, 42 model entries in four family labels (BIG-G T=0, BIG-G T=1, BIG-G sparse, GPT), 0-3 shots, temperatures 0 and 1.

Split and sample size: a seeded random row split with the paper's counts (43,049 / 10,763); the paper's split is unpublished (disclosed), and rows of one task and model fall on both sides (disclosed).

Inputs: training steps, batch size, total, non-embedding and FLOP-matched parameters, shots and temperature, not the task identity (disclosed); the paper speaks of model and dataset hyperparameters, and its Table 9 laws use training steps, number of shots and total parameters.

Metric and scoring: held-out MSE of the fitted law, as in Table 4 (constants fitted on the training set, MSE on the validation set). Locally the constants are fitted by a NumPy Levenberg-Marquardt routine from 8 starts with at most 5 constants; the paper's matrix of parameters and its monotonicity regulariser in training steps (A.6) are not reproduced, and the simplicity-accuracy Pareto frontier is replaced by the constant cap and source limits (all disclosed; the notes' 'per-group' reading of the matrix of parameters is their interpretation, the paper gives no detail).

Reported values: the notes quote Table 4 correctly (0.03598, 0.03610, 0.03598, 0.09324) and state that they are not reproduced (a constant reaches 0.0364 locally, Eq. 5 without refit 0.0367; recorded in the receipt). The paper's constant-model MSE of 0.09324 exceeds the local grade variance (0.0363) by far, which the local data cannot explain; not comparable (disclosed).

Selection: the held-out MSE is the score a search optimises, whereas the paper reports held-out MSEs only for the four laws of Table 4 and does not say whether its search saw the held-out rows. Not stated in the notes; corrected.

Search budget and method: the paper runs LaSR with 3840 populations of 200 candidates for 7 hours on 16 cores (the LLM used for this experiment is not named in Section 4.6 or A.6); the task fixes no search method or budget beyond 120 CPU seconds per fit, and the shipped config.yaml (OpenEvolve with google/gemini-2.5-flash) is unrelated to the paper's setup.

Not verified by me: the data rebuild and its SHA-256 lock, the reference MSEs and the saturation figures (recorded in validation/metaopt-checks.json; no evaluator was run), and the unit test comparing the NumPy Levenberg-Marquardt routine with scipy.optimize.least_squares.

Metadata (not a paper-relationship problem): task.json still has kind 'specification', evaluation.protocol 'specified_only', paper_direction null and validation.level 'paper_inventory'; requirements.notes ('Julia', 'LLM backend') are LaSR's requirements, not the local evaluator's; source_specification.description repeats the old description and source_specification.implementation_status is 'paper_inventory_only'.
applied_corrections: Corrected after this review: the description, which said 'This inventory specifies no executable scalar loss.', was rewritten to state the scaling_law interface, the least-squares fit on 43,049 rows and the held-out MSE on 10,763 rows.

Corrected after this review: the notes did not say that the held-out MSE is the score a search optimises, whereas the paper reports held-out MSEs only for the four laws of Table 4 and does not say whether its search saw the held-out rows.

source_associations.finding: EoB evolves benchmark-function programs that maximise a landscape similarity indicator (Eq. 3, NeurELA features, nearest target problem) and an algorithm distinguishing capability (Eq. 4, spread of a ten-algorithm pool's mean best values over B = 10 runs), and builds EoB-BBOB from 24 10-dimensional functions with CoCo-BBOB as the target. The local task scores one function with clean-room versions of both objectives (classical ELA features, local optimiser pool, local BBOB anchors) combined into one scalar; the substitutions are disclosed in the notes.

findings: Problem: EoB's objective pair (LSI and ADC, Section 3.2.2) with CoCo-BBOB as the target set is the experiment of Section 4.2 (EoB-BBOB). The task scores a single 10-dimensional function rather than a 24-function benchmark (disclosed).

LSI: Eq. 3 as printed (unsquared distance over sigma^2). NeurELA's 16-dimensional embedding is replaced by 16 classical exploratory-landscape-analysis features defined in metaopt_ela.py (not numerically identical to flacco) on a fixed 500-point Latin-hypercube sample; the targets are centroids of five instances of the suite's own BBOB implementation, not COCO's instances; sigma^2 and the feature scaling are local choices (the paper gives no value); the smaller LSI over the fixed and a candidate-specific shifted sample counts. All disclosed.

ADC: Eq. 4 with the min-max normalisation read as one normalisation of the whole 10 x 10 result matrix (disclosed as a reading; the paper does not say over which entries the minimum and maximum are taken). The paper's pool (Vanilla DE, JDE21, MadDE, NL-SHADE-LBC, PSO, GLPSO, sDMS-PSO, SAHLPSO, CMA-ES, Sep-CMA-ES) is replaced by local implementations of DE/rand/1/bin, jDE, JADE, L-SHADE, constriction PSO, ring PSO, CLPSO, DMS-PSO, CMA-ES and sep-CMA-ES; B = 10 runs as in the paper; 5,000 evaluations per run is a local choice (the paper states none). Disclosed.
Scalarisation: EoB treats LSI and ADC as two objectives (MOEA/D with PBI, theta = 5, N = 32); the score sqrt(LSI x min(1, ADC / 0.5)) is a suite convention (disclosed).
Domain: the paper states only that the EoB-BBOB functions are 10-dimensional; the [-5, 5]^10 box is BBOB's standard domain, and the notes attributed it to EoB-BBOB. Corrected in the notes.

Candidate interface: objective(X) on a batch of points, deterministic and batch-independent, matching the paper's vectorised GeneratedFunction programs in spirit; validity is only partly checked (valid = None) and the candidate runs in the evaluator process; the loopholes (copying a BBOB instance, recomputing the offset) are disclosed.

Search: the paper uses Deepseek-v3.2, 32 programs per generation, 10 generations and 2-3 runs; the task fixes no search method, and the shipped config.yaml (google/gemini-2.5-flash, OpenEvolve islands) is unrelated.
Reported values: the paper reports evolution curves and diversity plots, not numbers a local score could be compared with; the notes say scores are not comparable (disclosed).

Not verified by me: the reference checks in validation/metaopt-checks.json (LSI of unseen BBOB instances 0.30-0.75, nearest own function in 20 of 24, the seed's 0.356; no evaluator was run), the fidelity of the local optimisers to their publications and of the suite's BBOB functions to COCO.
