findings: Benchmark: EvoX (Table 3, Appendix A.2) and AdaEvolve (Table 2, Appendix B.1) both report the ADRS Telemetry Repair task with the human value 0.8222 / 0.822 and evolved scores of about 0.85-0.96. Neither releases the task: the pinned skydiscover tree (0d932b69, cached copy) has no telemetry directory under benchmarks/ADRS and its README marks Telemetry Repair 'Coming soon' (verified by me).

Evaluator provenance: the task ports evaluate_legacy of openevolve/examples/ADRS/telemetry_repair in UCB-ADRS/ADRS@259292f3; the original evaluate() first looks for a validation dataset that is not in that repository (disclosed). The receipt records that the unchanged original scores the ADRS reference program at 0.82218, the papers' human value, which supports but does not prove that the papers used this scoring path (disclosed as not established).

Data and sample size: 30 of the 40 Abilene rows drawn with seed 42, 30 directed interfaces of 12 routers, all statuses 'up'. I checked the prepared CSV: 40 rows, 787,281 bytes, 60 interface counter columns, 12 routers, timestamps from March to September 2004 (the notes said March 2004; corrected).

Metric and scoring: per-row 0.75 counter repair (1 - capped relative error over positive true counters) + 0.05 status accuracy + 0.2 confidence calibration, averaged over rows, as in the original; the receipt records agreement with the original to 1e-15 on three candidates (0.0511, 0.8385, 0.9434). EvoX calls the objective 'reconstruction accuracy' and AdaEvolve 'correctness and confidence calibration'.

Deviations, all disclosed: sandboxed child without pandas or scipy (the repository's reference programs do not run unchanged); ground-truth fields removed from correlated-bug interfaces; every interface must be returned with well-formed triples (the original skipped missing ones); perturbations from the evaluator's own random.Random(42) stream (the reference program scores 0.7994 on these fixed scenarios instead of 0.8222).

Headroom: echoing the measurements scores 0.838 and peer pairing 0.943, above the human value; the papers' best evolved programs reach about 0.95-0.96 (Table 3: 0.9520 EvoX/GPT-5, 0.9541 OpenEvolve/Gemini; Table 2 up to .960). Disclosed.

Task description: EvoX's Table 5 speaks of 'exploiting temporal and spatial correlations'; the scored snapshots are drawn in random order and scored independently, so only within-snapshot (peer) consistency is usable. This concerns EvoX's one-line summary rather than the ADRS evaluator, whose scoring path the task follows; noted, not corrected.

Search: both papers run 100 iterations with GPT-5 and Gemini-3(.0)-Pro, three runs; the task fixes no search method, and the shipped config.yaml (google/gemini-2.5-flash, OpenEvolve islands) is unrelated.

Not verified by me: the port-versus-original scores and the 0.8222 reproduction (recorded in validation/llm_tools-checks.json; no evaluator was run), the byte identity of the autoevolve and Engram copies, and the statement that the authors removed the example from the ADRS main branch.

The local task uses GEPA's HoVer setting with a different model, sample and candidate form; these settings are disclosed after this review's correction.

findings: Benchmark: all three papers evaluate HoVer multi-hop retrieval of gold Wikipedia documents: MIPRO (Tables 1-2, Recall@21), GEPA (Tables 1-2, HoverMultiHop) and the pairwise-validator paper (Table 2, through GEPA).

Retriever and corpus: bm25s (k1 0.9, b 0.4, English stopwords, Snowball stemmer) over the 5,233,330 2017 Wikipedia abstracts, as in GEPA's artifact per the notes; MIPRO's own retriever is not reproduced (disclosed). I checked the prepared files: 5,233,330 documents, 300 test claims each with three distinct gold titles, gold title coverage 1.0. The artifact code itself was not available to me.

Split and sample size: GEPA's 300 test claims, reconstructed from hover_train_release_v1.1.json by the artifact's procedure (identity with GEPA's files not checked, disclosed); a fixed 30-claim sample is scored, and candidates are optimised and scored on the same sample, so scores are in-sample (disclosed). GEPA reports on all 300 test claims after optimising on train/validation, MIPRO on 1,520 test claims, the pairwise-validator paper on 50.

Data selection: MIPRO keeps claims with 3 supporting facts (about 17% of its test claims need two documents), whereas the local claims are GEPA's three-document claims. Not stated in the notes; corrected.

Metric and scoring: a claim is solved when all its gold titles (dspy normalize_text) are among the retrieved titles, the score is the solved fraction; this matches GEPA's discrete_retrieval_eval per the notes, and MIPRO's Recall@21 with 21 = 3 hops of 7 (Listing 5, although Section 5.1 speaks of top-10 per hop). The local budget is 3 searches and 24 documents (GEPA's 7, 7 and 10), more than MIPRO's 21.

Candidate interface: the papers optimise prompts (and demonstrations) of a fixed DSPy program; here the whole solve(claim, search, llm) program is the candidate, within the retrieval budget, and only documents returned by search count (disclosed).

Model and budget: default google/gemini-2.5-flash at temperature 0, USD 0.5 per evaluation (disclosed); the papers use Llama-3-8B (MIPRO), Qwen3 8B and GPT-4.1 Mini (GEPA), Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-32B, Gemma-4-E4B and gpt-oss-20b (pairwise-validator, not mentioned in the notes before this review's correction).

Reported values: the seed (GEPA's program structure) scores 0.70 on the 30-claim sample (receipt), above GEPA's optimised HoVer test scores of 51.67% (GEPA) and 56.67% (GEPA+Merge) with GPT-4.1 Mini; model, sample and candidate form differ, and the notes state that no paper number is reproduced or comparable.

Not verified by me: the artifact details (bm25s versions, jax top-k, 7/7/10 retrieval, split code, discrete_retrieval_eval), the seed score and costs (validation/llm_tools-checks.json; no evaluator or model was run), and the dspy/cache and HoVer source revisions.

source_associations.finding: L-AutoDA evolves the generate function of an L2 random-walk decision-based attack (Algorithm 1, step size adapted by f(p)) on CIFAR-10 against Dadalto's ResNet-18, with the mean L2 distance on the first eight test images at 8,000 queries as fitness and mean L2 and success rate on 100 images per class at 2,500-10,000 queries as test results (Table 2). The local task uses the same model, framework and objective with a smaller default protocol (20 held-out images, 2,500 queries), different starting points and initial step size, all disclosed.

findings: Benchmark and model: Section 5.1 names CIFAR-10 and the ResNet-18 of Dadalto (2022), whose reference is huggingface.co/edadaltocg/resnet18_cifar10, the checkpoint used locally (revision ccacbae3); the receipt records 94.98% test accuracy, equal to the model card (not rerun by me). The pinned repository attacks RobustBench's WRN-28-10 instead (disclosed).

Framework: Algorithm 1's random walk with the paper's f(p) (0.5 + 2p up to p = 0.25, 5/6 + 2p/3 above), p <- 0.95 p + 0.05 k and s <- s f(p)^0.1, which I checked against step_factor and Attack.query in llm_tools_autoda.py; acceptance requires a misclassified proposal closer in L2, and the final examples are re-verified. The initial s is 0.05 (repository) instead of the paper's 0.001, selectable by s0 (disclosed).

Images and sample size: the default score uses 20 correctly classified held-out test images (2 per class, indices >= 8) at 2,500 queries, the paper's smallest test budget, instead of 100 images per class; the paper's evolution protocol (test images 0-7, 8,000 queries) is available as set='evolution' (disclosed). I checked attack_sets.json: the evolution set is test indices 0-7 and the held-out set 10 images per class.

Starting points: each image starts from the L2-nearest of 10 seeded test images that the model assigns to another class; the paper uses 'a set of 10 images with incorrect labels' without saying how one is chosen per image, and the repository searches a blended-noise start (disclosed).

Metric and scoring: mean final L2 distance (lower is better), the paper's fitness and the distance column of Table 2; the paper's success rate (L2 < 0.5) and median are reported as details only. Values are not comparable (disclosed): the seed, a Boundary-Attack-style move, scores 5.12 at 2,500 queries from an initial mean L2 of 13.85 (receipt), whereas Table 2 gives 1.9107 for the Boundary attack and 1.5202 for L-AutoDA-20 at 2,500 queries; the starting points and initial step size are the likely main causes (not verified).

Candidate interface: the draw_proposals signature that the notes attribute to the repository's task definition, called once per image per query in a sandbox without file or network access (numpy and the standard library); it never sees labels or the model. Noise comes from a seeded generator and no wall-clock abort enters the fitness (the repository aborts after 120 s); disclosed.

Search: the paper runs AEL for 20 generations of 10 candidates with GPT-3.5-turbo-1106; the task fixes no search method, and the shipped config.yaml (google/gemini-2.5-flash, OpenEvolve islands) is unrelated.

Not verified by me: the byte-identical cross-check against the repository's EvoAttack (4 x 200 and 8 x 1,500 queries) and the seed score (validation/llm_tools-checks.json; no evaluator was run), the repository details (EVOAttack_template.py, RobustBench default), which I could not read.

Kept limitation, possibly inaccurate: 'The matching pgg3/L-AutoDA repository has no README/license in the inspected tree; ...' while execution.commands cite README.md at the same commit as their source; not resolved here (the upgrade notes say only that there is no licence file).

Metadata (not a paper-relationship problem): task.json still has kind 'upstream', evaluation.protocol 'upstream' and validation.level 'source_inspected' (suite protocol 'recreated_verified'); execution.commands describe the upstream run_attack.py with a RobustBench download and the upstream LLM search; requirements.datasets ('100 randomly selected CIFAR-10 images per class and ResNet18 target') is the paper's protocol, not the local default.

source_associations.finding: HSI evaluates harness evolution on BALROG's BabyAI with DeepSeek-V4-Flash (Table 1: init harness 42.0, HSI 81.3 % Progress; 10 test episodes per task, 3 repeats). The local task plays BALROG BabyAI-Text through BALROG's own wrappers with HSI's task list and seed formula, scores mission completion over 10 fixed episodes, and replaces the evolved harness with a per-step act() policy and the backbone with gemini-2.5-flash; the differences are disclosed after this review's corrections.

findings: Benchmark: HSI evaluates on BALROG (Section 4.1) and reports BabyAI in Table 1 (Setup A): init harness 42.0 +- 3.5, meta-off 77.3, meta-on 81.3 % Progress with DeepSeek-V4-Flash; the paper does not list the BabyAI levels, which come from HSI's config per the notes (five BabyAI-MixedTrainLocal tasks: goto, pickup, open, putnext, pick_up_seq_go_to; TASKS in agent_bench_balrog.py).

Environment and protocol: agent_bench_balrog.py (read by me) runs BALROG's environments, instruction prompts and progression statistics in the pinned runtime, cleans replies to letters, spaces and colons, stops an episode when the last 12 valid actions form a strict period-2 or period-3 loop, and seeds episodes with int(sha256(f'{base_seed}_{suite}/{task}_{episode}_0')[:8], 16). That these rules are HSI's comes from the notes; HSI's code was not available to me.

Episodes and sample size: 2 seeded episodes per task (10 in all) with BALROG's level step limits, instead of HSI's 10 episodes per task with 3 test repeats (Appendix B.1 Table 3); disclosed. With 10 binary episodes the score moves in steps of 0.1.

findings: Benchmark: Section 4.1 and Appendix A.1 list ScienceWorld (Wang et al., 2022; interactive science tasks in which agents navigate rooms and run experiments) among AgentSquare's six tasks with 'progress rate' as metric; Table 1 reports 0.781 for AgentSquare with GPT-4o and Table A.3 0.432 with GPT-3.5. The paper names neither the variations nor a step limit; both come from AgentBoard's and AgentSquare's code.

Data and sample size: the prepared label file has 90 variations of 16 task types (34 easy, 56 hard; SHA-256 ed58212d..., equal to the data lock and to test.jsonl in the cached AgentSquare source). I recomputed the seeded SHA-256 sample: ids 72, 0, 66, 26, 73, 49, 63, 76, 51, 87, i.e. 8 of the 16 task types (find-living-thing and lifespan-longest-lived twice; 3 easy, 7 hard). Which variations the paper scored is not known (the AgentSquare repository also holds 30-, 20- and 5-variation subsets, which no code in the cached tasks/ tree references, and its error log fits the 30-variation one); the notes claimed all 90 and were corrected.

Episode protocol: agent_bench_sciworld.py reproduces AgentBoard's environment/scienceworld_env.py, which I compared with the cached AgentBoard source and AgentSquare's identical copy: the four simplifications, the first observation plus inventory, 'check valid actions' listing the simulator's action templates without 'reset', re.search matching of each open subgoal pattern after every step (matches stay), success and end when all match. As in AgentBoard's tasks/scienceworld.py loop, 'check valid actions' uses one of the 30 steps; valid_actions is always empty. The goal line uses AgentBoard's VanillaAgent wording ('You should perform actions to accomplish the goal') rather than AgentSquare's runner wording (minor).

Step budget: here every agent has at most 30 steps. In the AgentSquare source the 30-step bound (eval_main_sci.py default) applies only without a planning module; with one, each planned subtask gets up to 6 actions and the runner's loop applies no overall step cap, and the best searched SciWorld agent uses Voyager planning (Table A.4). Not disclosed before; corrected.

Simulator: scienceworld 1.2.1 is pinned; AgentBoard's and AgentSquare's requirements list 'scienceworld' without a version (I checked both), so the paper's simulator version is unknown. The simulator's JVM runs with -XX:hashCode=2 so that replays are identical; this fixes one processing order where default runs vary (disclosed as a deviation). Not verified by me: that 1.2.1 was the release current in July to October 2024, and the explanation that constant identity hashes make the simulator's collections iterate in insertion order. The JAR bundles Scala 2.12.9 (library.properties) and keeps object contents in Scala mutable Sets (javap of scienceworld.struct.EnvObject); Scala 2.12's mutable.HashTable prepends new entries to a bucket chain (javap of addEntry0), so insertion order does not hold for every hash collection; what the receipt establishes, and what scoring needs, is a reproducible order.

Metric and scoring: per episode the fraction of the variation's subgoal patterns matched so far, which never decreases, read at the episode's end (success, step cap, crash or timeout), averaged over the 10 episodes: AgentBoard's progress rate, the paper's metric. AgentBoard also reports success rate and easy/hard splits, which are only returned as details here.

source_associations.finding: LMX evolves make_walker() programs with LMX and MAP-Elites in OpenELM's Sodarace implementation, using the horizontal distance travelled after 1 second of simulation time as fitness and reporting niches, QD score and validity rate (Figure 11). The local task uses OpenELM's simulator with the spring assignment changed and a 28 s centre-of-mass displacement; LMX's 1 s setting was not mentioned in the notes and was added by this review.

findings: Objective: ELM defines Sodarace fitness as how far the centre of mass moves along the x-axis after a fixed time (Section 4), without stating the time; Stage 1 uses flat terrain (Section 5). LMX uses 'the distance travelled' (Section 4.5), measured after 1 second of simulation time (Appendix E). The local score is the absolute x displacement of the mass-weighted mean node position after 80 update_world(350) calls (I checked in sim_control_sodarace_sim.py that each call runs 21 Box2D steps of 1/60 s, i.e. 28 s, about 13 muscle periods of 2.1 s); absolute value, so motion in either direction counts. The duration is a local choice (disclosed; LMX's 1 s added by correction).

Simulator: the ELM authors' simulator is not public (disclosed); the evaluator vendors OpenELM's Python translation of iesor-physics at c844e149. I compared the cached OpenELM checkout: the loader's amplitude rule (cut-off 0.2 on (a + 1) / 2, amplitude 0.3 (a + 1) / 2), update_world (frame time capped at 0.35 s, speed-up 3) and evaluate (abs(min x + offsetX) after time // 350 updates; eval_ms default 1000) are as the notes state, and the iesor C++ addMuscleJoint overwrites the phase with the amplitude and constructs Muscle with swapped arguments, as stated. The receipt records identical node positions for OpenELM's seven seeds with OpenELM's muscle order.

Spring assignment (deviation, disclosed): amplitude and phase are assigned by name instead of OpenELM's swapped order, so dynamics differ from OpenELM's and hence from LMX's runs (receipt: e.g. wheel 17.9 vs 9.3, galloper -54.5 vs -15.9 units). Springs the ELM paper calls distance muscles (amplitude 0) oscillate here with amplitude 0.15, which they do not in OpenELM; added by correction.

Candidate interface: a make_walker() program using an injected walker_creator, as in ELM, built once in a sandboxed child; only joints and springs are returned. The injected creator is OpenELM's (two numeric add_muscle arguments, coordinates scaled by 0.22 with y flipped), not the one printed in the ELM paper (a boolean third argument; unscaled joints; amplitudes transformed to 2.12 in Figure 7; amplitudes up to 30 in Appendices F.2 and G.2), so the paper's programs do not run unchanged; added by correction. The local seed is ELM's square seed with the boolean dropped (as in OpenELM's square.py).

Validity: OpenELM's rules (amplitude at most 10 for every spring, at most 10 springs per joint, joints at least 0.003 apart) plus local caps (100 joints, 500 springs, 30 x 30 box, |phase| <= 1000, finite values) and rejection of runs where a node passes through the ground; I checked them in sim_control_sodarace.validate and simulate. ELM states that such limits exist but not their values.

Search and budget: ELM runs MAP-Elites with diff models (three runs per seed, 1,024,000 evaluations each, Section 5.1) and LMX 10,000 LMX iterations with CodeGen models; both report diversity (niches, QD score) as well as fitness. The local task scores a single walker by displacement only; MAP-Elites, the invention pipeline, terrains and QD scores are not reproduced (disclosed). No paper number is compared with.
Not verified by me: the seed score 0.79, the random-walker probe (median 3.5, maximum 40.9 units) and the OpenELM cross-check in validation/sim_control-checks.json; no simulator or evaluator was run.

findings: Benchmark and objective: Section 4.4 evolves Stable Diffusion prompts for three fitness functions, excess red, green and blue; excess red is the red-channel sum minus half the green and blue sums over the 8-bit RGB image (Appendix D gives the maximum 512 x 512 x 255 = 66,846,720). lmx_sd.excess_color computes this sum in float32 for channel 'r' on the full 512 x 512 uint8 image (I read the code); the score is the raw sum, as in the paper's fitness.

Rendering settings: Appendix D states SD v1.4 in its fp16 variant through diffusers, 512 x 512, 10 diffusion steps and the default NSFW filter (black image when triggered); lmx_sd.load_pipeline and GENERATION use the same, with the fp16 checkpoint at revision 2880f2ca, the checkpoint's PNDM scheduler, guidance 7.5, legacy attention and TF32 disabled. Section 4.4 reseeds a fixed PRNG seed before each render; the value 99 comes from the upstream script per the notes (not verified by me: jal278/lmx scripts/stablediffusion.py is not cached). Package versions differ from the paper's (disclosed: scores not comparable).

Candidate interface and budget: the paper evolves populations of 50 prompts for 100 generations (5,000 evaluations per run, three runs per colour) with Pythia-deduped 2.8B LMX offspring of at most 75 tokens, starting from lexica.art prompts; locally candidate() returns one prompt (at most 4096 bytes, truncated by the SD tokenizer at 77 tokens) that is scored once, and the seed program returns the neutral prompt 'A photograph of a landscape.' Disclosed in the notes as belonging to the search method.
Single fixed seed: as in the paper, the score is that of one image from one fixed latent, so a search can tune a prompt to that latent; the notes say so and give held-out-seed diagnostics.

Reported results: the paper reports normalised fitness curves (Figure 10; Section 4.4 describes a per-seed min-max normalisation, Appendix D a division by the maximum fitness) and the best prompts, with no table value; the local task embeds no paper number, and normalized_excess (score / 66,846,720) is display-only.

Device paths: the canonical GPU path (Linux, one CUDA device) and an optional CPU float32 path whose CPU-generated latents give different images, labelled with a separate protocol id and stated to be not comparable (seed prompt, red: 143,520 on Arena's GPU probe, 17,749 on the CPU). I confirmed in lmx_sd_cpu.py that only the device and its random generator, the dtype (exact float32 upcast of the fp16 weights), the CPU builds of torch and torchvision, the thread count and the macOS address-space limit differ.

source_associations.finding: RankEvolve evolves lexical ranking programs with the fitness 0.8 x Recall@100 + 0.2 x nDCG@10 and evaluates them on BEIR, BRIGHT and TREC DL; Climate-FEVER is one of its 16 held-out generalization datasets. The local task scores one candidate module on this dataset alone with RankEvolve's byte-identical binary metrics, interface and freeform seed, on the full corpus and all test queries; the single-dataset, search-on-test use is disclosed after this review's corrections.

findings: Benchmark and role: Section 4.2 evaluates 14 BEIR datasets (BioASQ, Signal-1M, TREC-NEWS, Robust04 and MS MARCO excluded) and names the 6 used during evolution; Climate-FEVER is not named, but by elimination it is one of the 8 held-out BEIR datasets (the repository README's evolution exclusion list names it), used only to test generalization, and Table 1 reports only the macro-average over the 8. Here a search optimises on it directly (search-on-test is disclosed; the paper's held-out role was added to the notes by this review).

Data: prepare.py reads the official BEIR archive (MD5 checked against contract.py), joins title and text and keeps the test queries in qrel order, as RankEvolve's loader does (I compared the cached repository); 5,416,593 documents and 1,535 queries, matching the counts in contract.py. Data state: dataset-lock.json pins the prepared manifest Arena reviewed (4614d0e4...), checked before and after the candidate runs.

Metric and scoring: per query Recall@100 and nDCG@10 with binary gains (any judgment above 0 is relevant), combined as 0.8 x Recall@100 + 0.2 x nDCG@10 and averaged over the queries with at least one positive in-corpus judgment. metrics.py is byte-identical to RankEvolve's tasks/_shared/metrics.py at 8f664bcd (I compared the SHA-256), and the upstream loader also keeps only judgments above 0 and skips queries without them. The paper gives the formula (averaged across datasets) but not whether nDCG is graded; the notes state the binary semantics and that it is not standard graded nDCG.

Candidate interface: RankEvolve's freeform-seed interface (BM25, Corpus, tokenize, LuceneTokenizer; rank(query_tokens, top_k=100)); the seed is the paper's main-experiment freeform seed, byte-identical to tasks/bm25/seeds/freeform.py inside the EVOLVE-BLOCK lines, with its pure-Python Lucene-style tokenizer (I checked the seed and the two tokenizer spans of seed_library.py against the cached repository). The candidate runs in a child that sees only public corpus and query files; rankings are validated (unique in-range indices, finite descending scores) and cut to 100.

Search and model: the paper evolves with OpenEvolve and GPT-5.2 at temperature 0.85 for 300 steps from the BM25 seed (Section 4.2); that is the method under study, the task fixes no search, and the shipped config.yaml (google/gemini-2.5-flash) is unrelated. The paper does not say whether evolution scored all or sampled queries; the repository evaluator's docstring lists EVAL_SAMPLE_QUERIES=20 among its OpenEvolve settings, while here every test query is scored (sample_queries=0, disclosed).

Budget: the candidate child has 14,400 s (dataset-lock.json) to tokenize, index and rank, with one thread (OMP and BM25_QUERY_WORKERS set to 1); the paper sets no time limit and reports latency only as averages over its 28 datasets on unstated hardware (Table 3: BM25 1.79 ms per document and 56.72 ms per query, best evolved BM25 2.81 and 648.89). Applied naively to 5,416,593 documents and 1,535 queries these give about 9,783 s and 16,217 s; the second exceeds the limit, so a program as slow as the paper's best may not finish within it (indicative only; the notes say a full-corpus seed run must still be measured).

Not verified by me: no full-corpus evaluation exists here; validation/arena-backport-checks.json records that the seed fails for missing prepared data (the scidocs download failed twice) and that Arena records no seed result; byte identity with Arena's evaluator, seed and lock is recorded there, not checked by me.

Metadata (not a paper-relationship problem; not corrected by this review's files): task.json still has kind 'upstream', evaluation.protocol 'upstream', validation.level 'source_inspected', and requirements and execution notes for the upstream evaluator (Java 21 and Pyserini, datasets/beir paths, 40-65 GB RAM, BM25/QL-Dir seeds), which the recreated evaluator does not use.
applied_corrections: Corrected after this review: the description ('climate-fever task evaluated in RankEvolve: Automating the Discovery of Retrieval Algorithms via LLM-Driven Evolution.') named only the dataset and the paper; it was rewritten to state the module interface, the corpus and queries, and the binary Recall/nDCG score.
Corrected after this review: the notes did not state the dataset's role in the paper (held out from evolution and used only to test generalization).

Data: prepare.py reads the official BEIR archive (MD5 checked against contract.py), joins title and text and keeps the test queries in qrel order, as RankEvolve's loader does (I compared the cached repository); 171,332 documents and 50 queries, matching the counts in contract.py. Data state: dataset-lock.json pins the prepared manifest Arena reviewed (8ff87a98...), checked before and after the candidate runs.

Metric and scoring: per query Recall@100 and nDCG@10 with binary gains (any judgment above 0 is relevant), combined as 0.8 x Recall@100 + 0.2 x nDCG@10 and averaged over the queries with at least one positive in-corpus judgment. metrics.py is byte-identical to RankEvolve's tasks/_shared/metrics.py at 8f664bcd (I compared the SHA-256), and the upstream loader also keeps only judgments above 0 and skips queries without them. The paper gives the formula (averaged across datasets) but not whether nDCG is graded; the notes state the binary semantics and that it is not standard graded nDCG.

Candidate interface: RankEvolve's freeform-seed interface (BM25, Corpus, tokenize, LuceneTokenizer; rank(query_tokens, top_k=100)); the seed is the paper's main-experiment freeform seed, byte-identical to tasks/bm25/seeds/freeform.py inside the EVOLVE-BLOCK lines, with its pure-Python Lucene-style tokenizer (I checked the seed and the two tokenizer spans of seed_library.py against the cached repository). The candidate runs in a child that sees only public corpus and query files; rankings are validated (unique in-range indices, finite descending scores) and cut to 100.

Search and model: the paper evolves with OpenEvolve and GPT-5.2 at temperature 0.85 for 300 steps from the BM25 seed (Section 4.2); that is the method under study, the task fixes no search, and the shipped config.yaml (google/gemini-2.5-flash) is unrelated. The paper does not say whether evolution scored all or sampled queries; the repository evaluator's docstring lists EVAL_SAMPLE_QUERIES=20 among its OpenEvolve settings, while here every test query is scored (sample_queries=0, disclosed).

Budget: the candidate child has 3,600 s (dataset-lock.json) to tokenize, index and rank, with one thread (OMP and BM25_QUERY_WORKERS set to 1); the paper sets no time limit and reports latency only as averages over its 28 datasets on unstated hardware (Table 3: BM25 1.79 ms per document and 56.72 ms per query, best evolved BM25 2.81 and 648.89). Applied naively to 171,332 documents and 50 queries these give about 310 s and 514 s; both fit within the limit (indicative only; the notes say a full-corpus seed run must still be measured).

Not verified by me: no full-corpus evaluation exists here; validation/arena-backport-checks.json records that the seed fails for missing prepared data (the scidocs download failed twice) and that Arena records no seed result; byte identity with Arena's evaluator, seed and lock is recorded there, not checked by me.

findings: Benchmark and data: DGM (Section 4.2), GEA (Section 4.1) and HyperAgents (Section 4.2, Appendix C.1) evaluate Aider Polyglot. The task uses the pinned polyglot-benchmark (225 Exercism exercises in six languages) and DGM's subset files. I compared the cached DGM small.json and medium.json (a565fd2d) with the lists of DGM Appendix E.3 and HyperAgents Appendix C.1: the 10 ids (2 Go, 2 Python, 2 JavaScript, 2 Rust, 1 C++, 1 Java) and the 50 ids are identical, in the same order, and the 50 include python__dominoes from the small list (59 distinct exercises), as the notes say. GEA's paper does not list its 10-task small set.

Split and sample size: only the 10-exercise first stage is scored (DGM: a functionality gate; GEA: its only evolution set; HyperAgents: initial training tasks), so the score moves in steps of 0.1 (disclosed). The papers report other sets: DGM 14.0% to 38.0% on its subsets and 14.2% to 30.7% on the full benchmark; HyperAgents 0.140 to 0.340 on the 50-task subset and 0.084 to 0.267 on the full benchmark; GEA 38.2% to 88.3%. The gate is 'over 40%' in DGM's text and >= 40% in self_improve_step.py (I checked the cached code), as the notes say. HyperAgents gives 165 test tasks; the two DGM lists hold 59 distinct exercises, so 166 remain (the local 'heldout'); I did not check which 165 it used.

Model: DGM evaluates Polyglot agents with o3-mini at temperature 1.0 (Appendix D.1, Table 3), HyperAgents adopts the same (Appendix D.1), GEA uses Claude Haiku 4.5 and then Claude Sonnet 4.5 for its acting module (Section 4.2). The local client defaults to google/gemini-2.5-flash at temperature 0 (llm.py). DGM's setting was disclosed; GEA's and HyperAgents' were added by correction. No paper number is reproduced or compared as a target.

Candidate interface: DGM's base agent works in the task container with a Bash tool and an edit tool (Section 4.1) and runs up to 600 s (timeout 600 in the cached polyglot/harness.py); GEA and HyperAgents evolve such tool-using agents. Locally solve(exercise, llm) runs in a sandboxed child without file, process or network access, sees the instructions, stubs and a few build files as text, cannot execute code, may only return solution files (validate_files), and has 300 s wall-clock, 120 s CPU and 512 MB. Disclosed in the Agent interface and Budget notes.

Metric and scoring: pass@1 without test feedback, as all three papers report (DGM Section 4.2 and Appendix E.5, GEA Section 4.1, HyperAgents Appendix C.1). An exercise is solved when the test command exits 0, as in DGM's harness (checked), plus a framework-summary guard (polyglot_runner.summary); an unchanged stub is not tested and scores 0, as DGM's empty-patch rule (checked). The test commands equal DGM's constants.py (checked); the 180 s limit and the @Disabled removal follow Aider's benchmark.py (checked) rather than DGM (120 s, Java tests with @Disabled skipped), which makes Java stricter than in DGM; disclosed in the Tests note.

Budget: the default USD 0.50 per evaluation is split over the 10 exercises (0.05 each). The papers state no per-task spending cap; their cost estimates are about USD 5 for 60 Polyglot tasks with o3-mini (DGM Appendix E.1), 0.89M o3-mini tokens for 60 tasks (HyperAgents Appendix D.2) and USD 20 (Haiku) to 60 (Sonnet) per 60 tasks (GEA Appendix A.1). The search budgets (DGM 80 iterations; GEA 20 iterations of groups of 2; HyperAgents 80 iterations for Polyglot) belong to the method under study and are not fixed by the task; the shipped config.yaml is unrelated.

Not verified by me (no evaluator was run): the receipt's reference check (225/225 reference solutions pass, 219/225 stubs fail), the image build and toolchain versions, the seed scores (0.5, 0.4 and 0.4 on fresh runs; 0.26 on DGM's 50-exercise list), the data lock and the licence statements; also whether GEA's small set equals DGM's list.

The top-level limitations list is empty, so no limitation is superseded; the merged record hyperagents-aider-polyglot still carries its historical implementation-gap sentence.

findings: Benchmark and task: LIMEN evaluates XLand-MiniGrid Easy: pick up a specified object in a 9 x 9 grid with distractors, 80-step horizon (Section 5.1); Appendix D.1 names the blue pyramid. Protocol and budget: as in the paper's in-search fitness (Section 5.3, Appendix A.1 Tables 1 and 3) and LIMEN's YAML, a 500,000-step cascade run with seed 42 must reach 5 %, then PPO with seeds 42, 43 and 44 for 1,000,000 steps (7 updates, 917,504 steps), 50 fitness episodes per seed, 80-step evaluation horizon. Metric and scoring: the score is the test MAE averaged over the 9 test conditions and over steps 1-32 (jax_station_zap_score.score: mean of per-condition MAEs over windows, steps and neurons), the 'Average' of Fig. 8. From the cached combined.json I recomputed the context-4 values the notes cite (mean 0.03186, linear 0.02924, TSMixer 0.02814, UNet 0.02676, means over 3 runs where available).

Budget and seeds (proxy): one seed (42) and at most 3 epochs or 600 s of CPU training with four threads, instead of 3 seeds and up to 120 epochs or 60 minutes per run on a Ray cluster of 40 GPUs (Section 3.3, Appendix B; the Station's task text gives 24 GB per GPU). Candidate interface: the Station's hooks (create_network with init/apply and optional mutable and needs_rng, compute_loss, create_optimizer, _define_hyperparameters, BATCH_SIZE) as in its research_task.md, with omitted hooks falling back to a port of defaults.py (I compared the seed with the cached defaults.py: shared-neuron MLP 4 -> 64 -> 32 with BatchNorm and Dropout 0.1, MAE loss, Adam). findings: Benchmark and task: EvoPrompting (Section 4.2) evaluates on the CLRS benchmark of 30 algorithms and reports, in Appendix A.6 Table 3, the OOD accuracy and model size of the best of five discovered Triplet-GMPNN variants and of the Triplet-GMPNN baseline for every algorithm, Activity Selector included. The paper ran no search on Activity Selector: its Table 3 entry evaluates models found on articulation points, Graham scan and Kruskal's MST (disclosed in the Source protocol note). The task trains the CLRS encode-process-decode network (a PyTorch port of dm-clrs 2.0.3) around a candidate processor on this algorithm and scores the CLRS-30 test split. The CLRS benchmark paper (arXiv 2205.15659) and Ibarz et al. (arXiv 2209.11142) are not in .cache/primary-paper-text; I checked the CLRS facts below in the dm-clrs 2.0.3 source instead.

Data, split and sample size: CLRS-30 v1.0.0, the archive dm-clrs's dataset.py names; I checked in samplers.py that its splits are 1000 training trajectories of length 16, and 32 validation (length 16) and 32 test (length 64) samples times the algorithm's multiplier in specs.CLRS_30_ALGS_SETTINGS (1 for activity_selector). The data lock lists 1000/32/32 samples with 16/16/64 nodes for activity_selector.npz, and the evaluator uses 32 validation and 32 test samples (clrs_data.spread takes evenly spaced subsets when fewer than all samples are used). dm-clrs run.py instead samples fresh training trajectories of sizes 4, 7, 11, 13 and 16 and fresh validation samples of size 16 (with randomised pos), and reads only the test split from the archive (create_samplers, checked); disclosed in the Data note, except the minor point that local validation keeps the archive's unrandomised pos (it only affects which checkpoint is restored).

Candidate interface: build_processor(hidden_dim) returns a torch module called once per algorithm step with node, edge and graph features, the adjacency and the previous hidden state, returning node embeddings and optionally edge embeddings, the processor's role in dm-clrs nets.py. The paper's search changed only the triplet-message function of a Triplet-GMPNN (Section 4.2); the candidate may replace the whole processor (a superset; disclosed). I compared the seed with dm-clrs processors.py (MPNN with an all-ones adjacency, message MLP [128, 128], max aggregation, layer norm, gate with bias -3, 8 triplet features, o3 with ReLU): it is the triplet_gmpnn processor, and the receipt's seed network has 262,204 parameters (258,872 in the processor), equal to Table 3's baseline size 262,204 (tests/test_clrs_training.py asserts this for all 30 algorithms; I checked the 17 sizes of this package against the cached Table 3).

Metric and scoring: the score is the mean over the algorithm's output probes of dm-clrs's evaluate metric on hard predictions; Activity Selector has one output, selected (node mask), so the score is the F1 of the predicted selection over all test nodes (threshold 0 on the logits). I compared clrs_metrics.mask_f1 with dm-clrs evaluation._mask_fn (micro-averaged tp, fp, fn; precision and recall 1 when undefined) and the probe types with dm-clrs specs.SPECS. Direction maximize, range [0, 1]; the test outputs stay in the scoring process (clrs_eval.visible_splits).

Budget: 1200 Adam updates (60 % of the paper's 2000-step search budget per child model), learning rate 1e-3, batch 32, gradient clipping 1.0, hidden size 128 (dm-clrs run.py's single-task defaults, which I checked; run.py trains for 10,000 steps), validation every 50 updates with the best checkpoint restored, one training seed (0), CPU with 4 threads, 1700 s wall-clock and 3584 MB memory limits. The paper's search used AdamW on one P100 GPU; Table 3 states no training length or hardware (Reference checks note corrected). The notes disclose that the local scores are far below and not comparable with the published ones.

Objective: the paper's search fitness is -(model size x best validation error) after 2000 steps (Section 3.3; Eval returns the lowest validation error), and the paper reports the OOD accuracy of selected models; the local score is the test score itself, out of distribution, with a 1,000,000-parameter processor cap and no size term, so a search optimises on the reported test split (disclosed in the Objective note).

Reported values: Table 3 lists for Activity Selector the best model 'Baseline' (262,204 parameters) at 95.05 +- 0.53 %, EvoPrompting's Triplet-GMPNN at 93.96 +- 0.29 % and Ibarz et al.'s at 95.18 +- 0.45 % (baseline size 262,204); the Reference checks note quotes them correctly (compared with the cached text). Table 3 gives the 'Baseline' best model a different accuracy (95.05 %) than its own Triplet-GMPNN column (93.96 %) without explanation; the note copies both as printed.

Seed and discrimination (receipt, not re-run by me): on 2026-10-11 (1-minute load 9.78) the seed scores 0.8263 in 516 s, far below Table 3's 93.96 % as the notes say, and a processor without message passing scores 0.5890, a margin of 0.2374; the variation across training seeds was not measured for this task. A processor returning the wrong shape and a program importing os were rejected (receipt).

Not verified by me (no evaluator was run): the measured values in the notes and validation/clrs-checks.json (seed, reference and repeat scores, timings, memory, determinism, rejection of invalid candidates), the TFRecord conversion of scripts/prepare_clrs.py and the content digests of catalog/clrs-data-lock.json, and that the PyTorch port reproduces dm-clrs numerically (the notes say it was not cross-checked; I compared by reading the processor, metrics, hint post-processing and data options named above). The paper calls its metric 'OOD accuracy' without defining it; that it equals the CLRS evaluate score is inferred from its use of Ibarz et al.'s setup. The venue (NeurIPS 2023) is not stated in the cached arXiv v3 text.

Parameter count is minimized.') describes the paper's search, not the local score. source_associations.finding: EvoPrompting reports, in Appendix A.6 Table 3, the OOD accuracy on CLRS-30 BFS of its best discovered model (MaxMean, 99.99 %), of its own Triplet-GMPNN (99.80 %) and of Ibarz et al.'s (99.73 %), after training whose length the paper does not state; its search ran on three other algorithms with a validation-error x model-size fitness after 2000 steps on a P100 GPU. The local task is a reduced-budget proxy: one 1500-step CPU training of the candidate processor scored on the same CLRS-30 test split with the CLRS metric, no size term; the differences are disclosed after this review's corrections.

findings: Benchmark and task: EvoPrompting (Section 4.2) evaluates on the CLRS benchmark of 30 algorithms and reports, in Appendix A.6 Table 3, the OOD accuracy and model size of the best of five discovered Triplet-GMPNN variants and of the Triplet-GMPNN baseline for every algorithm, BFS included. The paper ran no search on BFS: its Table 3 entry evaluates models found on articulation points, Graham scan and Kruskal's MST (disclosed in the Source protocol note). The task trains the CLRS encode-process-decode network (a PyTorch port of dm-clrs 2.0.3) around a candidate processor on this algorithm and scores the CLRS-30 test split. The CLRS benchmark paper (arXiv 2205.15659) and Ibarz et al. (arXiv 2209.11142) are not in .cache/primary-paper-text; I checked the CLRS facts below in the dm-clrs 2.0.3 source instead.

Data, split and sample size: CLRS-30 v1.0.0, the archive dm-clrs's dataset.py names; I checked in samplers.py that its splits are 1000 training trajectories of length 16, and 32 validation (length 16) and 32 test (length 64) samples times the algorithm's multiplier in specs.CLRS_30_ALGS_SETTINGS (1 for bfs). The data lock lists 1000/32/32 samples with 16/16/64 nodes for bfs.npz, and the evaluator uses 32 validation and 32 test samples (clrs_data.spread takes evenly spaced subsets when fewer than all samples are used). dm-clrs run.py instead samples fresh training trajectories of sizes 4, 7, 11, 13 and 16 and fresh validation samples of size 16 (with randomised pos), and reads only the test split from the archive (create_samplers, checked); disclosed in the Data note, except the minor point that local validation keeps the archive's unrandomised pos (it only affects which checkpoint is restored).

Candidate interface: build_processor(hidden_dim) returns a torch module called once per algorithm step with node, edge and graph features, the adjacency and the previous hidden state, returning node embeddings and optionally edge embeddings, the processor's role in dm-clrs nets.py. The paper's search changed only the triplet-message function of a Triplet-GMPNN (Section 4.2); the candidate may replace the whole processor (a superset; disclosed). I compared the seed with dm-clrs processors.py (MPNN with an all-ones adjacency, message MLP [128, 128], max aggregation, layer norm, gate with bias -3, 8 triplet features, o3 with ReLU): it is the triplet_gmpnn processor, and the receipt's seed network has 523,963 parameters (258,872 in the processor), equal to Table 3's baseline size 523,963 (tests/test_clrs_training.py asserts this for all 30 algorithms; I checked the 17 sizes of this package against the cached Table 3).

Metric and scoring: the score is the mean over the algorithm's output probes of dm-clrs's evaluate metric on hard predictions; BFS has one output, pi (node pointer: each node's BFS-tree predecessor), so the score is the fraction of the 32 x 64 test nodes whose predicted pointer (argmax over nodes) is correct. I compared clrs_metrics.probe_score with dm-clrs evaluation.py (pointer equality, micro-averaged over all samples) and the probe types with dm-clrs specs.SPECS. Direction maximize, range [0, 1]; the test outputs stay in the scoring process (clrs_eval.visible_splits).

Budget: 1500 Adam updates (75 % of the paper's 2000-step search budget per child model), learning rate 1e-3, batch 32, gradient clipping 1.0, hidden size 128 (dm-clrs run.py's single-task defaults, which I checked; run.py trains for 10,000 steps), validation every 50 updates with the best checkpoint restored, one training seed (0), CPU with 4 threads, 1700 s wall-clock and 3584 MB memory limits. The paper's search used AdamW on one P100 GPU; Table 3 states no training length or hardware (Reference checks note corrected). The Budget note said the local scores are far below the published ones, which is not the case for this algorithm; it was corrected (the scores remain not comparable).

Objective: the paper's search fitness is -(model size x best validation error) after 2000 steps (Section 3.3; Eval returns the lowest validation error), and the paper reports the OOD accuracy of selected models; the local score is the test score itself, out of distribution, with a 1,000,000-parameter processor cap and no size term, so a search optimises on the reported test split (disclosed in the Objective note).

Reported values: Table 3 lists for BFS the best model MaxMean (522,931 parameters) at 99.99 +- 0.01 %, EvoPrompting's Triplet-GMPNN at 99.80 +- 0.04 % and Ibarz et al.'s at 99.73 +- 0.04 % (baseline size 523,963); the Reference checks note quotes them correctly (compared with the cached text). The paper's values are at the ceiling, and so is the local task: the seed already scores about 0.99, so little headroom is left (not stated in the notes; not a difference from the paper).

Seed and discrimination (receipt, not re-run by me): on 2026-10-11 (1-minute load 10.97) the seed scores 0.9883 in 571 s and a processor without message passing scores 0.9429, a margin of 0.0454. Because that processor scores at least 0.90, the package's saturation rule was applied: with training seeds 0, 1 and 2 the seed scores 0.9883, 0.9922, 0.9946 (standard deviation 0.0032, which I recomputed as the sample standard deviation), and the margin exceeds two standard deviations, as the Reference checks note says; the variation of the no-message-passing processor across seeds was not measured. A processor returning the wrong shape and a program importing os were rejected (receipt).

Not verified by me (no evaluator was run): the measured values in the notes and validation/clrs-checks.json (seed, reference and repeat scores, timings, memory, determinism, rejection of invalid candidates), the TFRecord conversion of scripts/prepare_clrs.py and the content digests of catalog/clrs-data-lock.json, and that the PyTorch port reproduces dm-clrs numerically (the notes say it was not cross-checked; I compared by reading the processor, metrics, hint post-processing and data options named above). The paper calls its metric 'OOD accuracy' without defining it; that it equals the CLRS evaluate score is inferred from its use of Ibarz et al.'s setup. The venue (NeurIPS 2023) is not stated in the cached arXiv v3 text.

Metadata (not a paper-relationship problem): task.json still has kind 'specification', evaluation.protocol 'specified_only', validation.level 'paper_inventory' (adapter_checks null), source_specification.implementation_status 'paper_inventory_only', requirements.hardware 'See upstream requirements and task notes.' and labels.cost 'not_run', although the suite protocol is 'recreated' and runs on the CPU; execution.notes ('... Parameter count is minimized.') describes the paper's search, not the local score. The three limitations stay: EvoPrompting released no code, so no official or paper-linked repository exists (the evaluator ports dm-clrs instead), and the paper's GPU search and training were not run.

Candidate interface: build_processor(hidden_dim) returns a torch module called once per algorithm step with node, edge and graph features, the adjacency and the previous hidden state, returning node embeddings and optionally edge embeddings, the processor's role in dm-clrs nets.py. The paper's search changed only the triplet-message function of a Triplet-GMPNN (Section 4.2); the candidate may replace the whole processor (a superset; disclosed). I compared the seed with dm-clrs processors.py (MPNN with an all-ones adjacency, message MLP [128, 128], max aggregation, layer norm, gate with bias -3, 8 triplet features, o3 with ReLU): it is the triplet_gmpnn processor, and the receipt's seed network has 525,886 parameters (258,872 in the processor), equal to Table 3's baseline size 525,886 (tests/test_clrs_training.py asserts this for all 30 algorithms; I checked the 17 sizes of this package against the cached Table 3).

Metric and scoring: the score is the mean over the algorithm's output probes of dm-clrs's evaluate metric on hard predictions; Dijkstra has one output, pi (node pointer: each node's predecessor on its shortest path), so the score is the fraction of the 32 x 64 test nodes whose predicted pointer (argmax over nodes) is correct. I compared clrs_metrics.probe_score with dm-clrs evaluation.py (pointer equality, micro-averaged over all samples) and the probe types with dm-clrs specs.SPECS. Direction maximize, range [0, 1]; the test outputs stay in the scoring process (clrs_eval.visible_splits).

Budget: 800 Adam updates (40 % of the paper's 2000-step search budget per child model), learning rate 1e-3, batch 32, gradient clipping 1.0, hidden size 128 (dm-clrs run.py's single-task defaults, which I checked; run.py trains for 10,000 steps), validation every 50 updates with the best checkpoint restored, one training seed (0), CPU with 4 threads, 1700 s wall-clock and 3584 MB memory limits. The paper's search used AdamW on one P100 GPU; Table 3 states no training length or hardware (Reference checks note corrected). The notes disclose that the local scores are far below and not comparable with the published ones.

Objective: the paper's search fitness is -(model size x best validation error) after 2000 steps (Section 3.3; Eval returns the lowest validation error), and the paper reports the OOD accuracy of selected models; the local score is the test score itself, out of distribution, with a 1,000,000-parameter processor cap and no size term, so a search optimises on the reported test split (disclosed in the Objective note).

Reported values: Table 3 lists for Dijkstra the best model Div2Mean (524,854 parameters) at 97.30 +- 0.28 %, EvoPrompting's Triplet-GMPNN at 95.94 +- 0.66 % and Ibarz et al.'s at 96.05 +- 0.60 % (baseline size 525,886); the Reference checks note quotes them correctly (compared with the cached text).

findings: Benchmark and task: EvoPrompting (Section 4.2) evaluates on the CLRS benchmark of 30 algorithms and reports, in Appendix A.6 Table 3, the OOD accuracy and model size of the best of five discovered Triplet-GMPNN variants and of the Triplet-GMPNN baseline for every algorithm, Graham Scan included. Graham Scan is one of the three algorithms on which the paper ran its search (Section 4.2, Figure 3), with the search fitness on validation data; its Table 3 entry is the OOD accuracy of the best discovered model and of the baseline. The task trains the CLRS encode-process-decode network (a PyTorch port of dm-clrs 2.0.3) around a candidate processor on this algorithm and scores the CLRS-30 test split. The CLRS benchmark paper (arXiv 2205.15659) and Ibarz et al. (arXiv 2209.11142) are not in .cache/primary-paper-text; I checked the CLRS facts below in the dm-clrs 2.0.3 source instead.

Data, split and sample size: CLRS-30 v1.0.0, the archive dm-clrs's dataset.py names; I checked in samplers.py that its splits are 1000 training trajectories of length 16, and 32 validation (length 16) and 32 test (length 64) samples times the algorithm's multiplier in specs.CLRS_30_ALGS_SETTINGS (1 for graham_scan). The data lock lists 1000/32/32 samples with 16/16/64 nodes for graham_scan.npz, and the evaluator uses 32 validation and 32 test samples (clrs_data.spread takes evenly spaced subsets when fewer than all samples are used). dm-clrs run.py instead samples fresh training trajectories of sizes 4, 7, 11, 13 and 16 and fresh validation samples of size 16 (with randomised pos), and reads only the test split from the archive (create_samplers, checked); disclosed in the Data note, except the minor point that local validation keeps the archive's unrandomised pos (it only affects which checkpoint is restored).

Candidate interface: build_processor(hidden_dim) returns a torch module called once per algorithm step with node, edge and graph features, the adjacency and the previous hidden state, returning node embeddings and optionally edge embeddings, the processor's role in dm-clrs nets.py. The paper's search changed only the triplet-message function of a Triplet-GMPNN (Section 4.2); the candidate may replace the whole processor (a superset; disclosed). I compared the seed with dm-clrs processors.py (MPNN with an all-ones adjacency, message MLP [128, 128], max aggregation, layer norm, gate with bias -3, 8 triplet features, o3 with ReLU): it is the triplet_gmpnn processor, and the receipt's seed network has 398,409 parameters (258,872 in the processor), equal to Table 3's baseline size 398,409 (tests/test_clrs_training.py asserts this for all 30 algorithms; I checked the 17 sizes of this package against the cached Table 3).

Metric and scoring: the score is the mean over the algorithm's output probes of dm-clrs's evaluate metric on hard predictions; Graham scan has one output, in_hull (node mask: whether a point is on the convex hull), so the score is the F1 of the predicted hull membership over all test points (threshold 0 on the logits). I compared clrs_metrics.mask_f1 with dm-clrs evaluation._mask_fn (micro-averaged tp, fp, fn; precision and recall 1 when undefined) and the probe types with dm-clrs specs.SPECS. Direction maximize, range [0, 1]; the test outputs stay in the scoring process (clrs_eval.visible_splits).

Budget: 150 Adam updates (8 % of the paper's 2000-step search budget per child model), learning rate 1e-3, batch 32, gradient clipping 1.0, hidden size 128 (dm-clrs run.py's single-task defaults, which I checked; run.py trains for 10,000 steps), validation every 18 updates with the best checkpoint restored, one training seed (0), CPU with 4 threads, 1700 s wall-clock and 3584 MB memory limits. The paper's search used AdamW on one P100 GPU; Table 3 states no training length or hardware (Reference checks note corrected). The notes disclose that the local scores are far below and not comparable with the published ones. Training recomputes each algorithm step in the backward pass (activation checkpointing; parameter checkpoint_steps), which changes memory and time, not values (claimed; tests/test_clrs_training.py compares losses and gradients; not run by me).

Objective: the paper's search fitness is -(model size x best validation error) after 2000 steps (Section 3.3; Eval returns the lowest validation error), and the paper reports the OOD accuracy of selected models; the local score is the test score itself, out of distribution, with a 1,000,000-parameter processor cap and no size term, so a search optimises on the reported test split (disclosed in the Objective note).

Reported values: Table 3 lists for Graham Scan the best model MaxMean (397,377 parameters) at 93.76 +- 0.85 %, EvoPrompting's Triplet-GMPNN at 92.72 +- 2.38 % and Ibarz et al.'s at 93.62 +- 0.91 % (baseline size 398,409); the Reference checks note quotes them correctly (compared with the cached text). Figure 3 shows the search on this algorithm only as fitness curves, and the paper does not say which of the five discovered models came from which of its three searches.

Seed and discrimination (receipt, not re-run by me): on 2026-10-10 (1-minute load 7.63) the seed scores 0.8110 in 161 s, below Table 3's 92.72 % as the notes say, and a processor without message passing scores 0.6072, a margin of 0.2037; the variation across training seeds was not measured for this task. A processor returning the wrong shape and a program importing os were rejected (receipt).

The paper calls its metric 'OOD accuracy' without defining it; that it equals the CLRS evaluate score is inferred from its use of Ibarz et al.'s setup. The local task is a reduced-budget proxy: one 1500-step CPU training of the candidate processor scored on the same CLRS-30 test split with the CLRS metric, no size term; the differences are disclosed after this review's corrections.

findings: Benchmark and task: EvoPrompting (Section 4.2) evaluates on the CLRS benchmark of 30 algorithms and reports, in Appendix A.6 Table 3, the OOD accuracy and model size of the best of five discovered Triplet-GMPNN variants and of the Triplet-GMPNN baseline for every algorithm, LCS Length included. The paper ran no search on LCS Length: its Table 3 entry evaluates models found on articulation points, Graham scan and Kruskal's MST (disclosed in the Source protocol note). The task trains the CLRS encode-process-decode network (a PyTorch port of dm-clrs 2.0.3) around a candidate processor on this algorithm and scores the CLRS-30 test split. The CLRS benchmark paper (arXiv 2205.15659) and Ibarz et al. (arXiv 2209.11142) are not in .cache/primary-paper-text; I checked the CLRS facts below in the dm-clrs 2.0.3 source instead.

Data, split and sample size: CLRS-30 v1.0.0, the archive dm-clrs's dataset.py names; I checked in samplers.py that its splits are 1000 training trajectories of length 16, and 32 validation (length 16) and 32 test (length 64) samples times the algorithm's multiplier in specs.CLRS_30_ALGS_SETTINGS (1 for lcs_length). The data lock lists 1000/32/32 samples with 16/16/64 nodes for lcs_length.npz, and the evaluator uses 32 validation and 32 test samples (clrs_data.spread takes evenly spaced subsets when fewer than all samples are used). dm-clrs run.py instead samples fresh training trajectories of sizes 4, 7, 11, 13 and 16 and fresh validation samples of size 16 (with randomised pos), and reads only the test split from the archive (create_samplers, checked); disclosed in the Data note, except the minor point that local validation keeps the archive's unrandomised pos (it only affects which checkpoint is restored).

Candidate interface: build_processor(hidden_dim) returns a torch module called once per algorithm step with node, edge and graph features, the adjacency and the previous hidden state, returning node embeddings and optionally edge embeddings, the processor's role in dm-clrs nets.py. The paper's search changed only the triplet-message function of a Triplet-GMPNN (Section 4.2); the candidate may replace the whole processor (a superset; disclosed). I compared the seed with dm-clrs processors.py (MPNN with an all-ones adjacency, message MLP [128, 128], max aggregation, layer norm, gate with bias -3, 8 triplet features, o3 with ReLU): it is the triplet_gmpnn processor, and the receipt's seed network has 270,419 parameters (258,872 in the processor), equal to Table 3's baseline size 270,419 (tests/test_clrs_training.py asserts this for all 30 algorithms; I checked the 17 sizes of this package against the cached Table 3).

Metric and scoring: the score is the mean over the algorithm's output probes of dm-clrs's evaluate metric on hard predictions; LCS Length has one output, b (edge categorical: the back-pointer class of each node pair), so the score is the argmax accuracy over the test node pairs whose one-hot truth has no -1 entry, i.e. the cells that pair a character of the first string with one of the second (dm-clrs probing.strings_pair_cat masks the others). I compared clrs_metrics.one_hot_accuracy with dm-clrs evaluation._eval_one and the probe types with dm-clrs specs.SPECS; the constant pred_h hint becomes an input (run.py PRED_AS_INPUT_ALGOS, checked). Direction maximize, range [0, 1]; the test outputs stay in the scoring process (clrs_eval.visible_splits).

Budget: 1500 Adam updates (75 % of the paper's 2000-step search budget per child model), learning rate 1e-3, batch 32, gradient clipping 1.0, hidden size 128 (dm-clrs run.py's single-task defaults, which I checked; run.py trains for 10,000 steps), validation every 50 updates with the best checkpoint restored, one training seed (0), CPU with 4 threads, 1700 s wall-clock and 3584 MB memory limits. The paper's search used AdamW on one P100 GPU; Table 3 states no training length or hardware (Reference checks note corrected). The Budget note said the local scores are far below the published ones, which is not the case for this algorithm; it was corrected (the scores remain not comparable).

Objective: the paper's search fitness is -(model size x best validation error) after 2000 steps (Section 3.3; Eval returns the lowest validation error), and the paper reports the OOD accuracy of selected models; the local score is the test score itself, out of distribution, with a 1,000,000-parameter processor cap and no size term, so a search optimises on the reported test split (disclosed in the Objective note).

Reported values: Table 3 lists for LCS Length the best model 'Baseline' (270,419 parameters) at 85.75 +- 0.80 %, EvoPrompting's Triplet-GMPNN at 86.05 +- 0.65 % and Ibarz et al.'s at 80.51 +- 1.84 % (baseline size 270,419); the Reference checks note quotes them correctly (compared with the cached text). Table 3's 'best' model 'Baseline' (85.75 %) scores below its own Triplet-GMPNN column (86.05 %) without explanation; the note copies both as printed.

Seed and discrimination (receipt, not re-run by me): on 2026-10-11 (1-minute load 9.63) the seed scores 0.8368 in 619 s, close to Table 3's 86.05 % and above Ibarz et al.'s 80.51 %, and a processor without message passing scores 0.8129, a margin of only 0.0239, whose variation across training seeds was not measured; the Reference checks note says so. With so small a margin the score separates message-passing from per-node processors weakly. A processor returning the wrong shape and a program importing os were rejected (receipt).

Not verified by me (no evaluator was run): the measured values in the notes and validation/clrs-checks.json (seed, reference and repeat scores, timings, memory, determinism, rejection of invalid candidates), the TFRecord conversion of scripts/prepare_clrs.py and the content digests of catalog/clrs-data-lock.json, and that the PyTorch port reproduces dm-clrs numerically (the notes say it was not cross-checked; I compared by reading the processor, metrics, hint post-processing and data options named above). The paper calls its metric 'OOD accuracy' without defining it; that it equals the CLRS evaluate score is inferred from its use of Ibarz et al.'s setup. The venue (NeurIPS 2023) is not stated in the cached arXiv v3 text.

Metadata (not a paper-relationship problem): task.json still has kind 'specification', evaluation.protocol 'specified_only', validation.level 'paper_inventory' (adapter_checks null), source_specification.implementation_status 'paper_inventory_only', requirements.hardware 'See upstream requirements and task notes.' and labels.cost 'not_run', although the suite protocol is 'recreated' and runs on the CPU; execution.notes ('... Parameter count is minimized.') describes the paper's search, not the local score. The three limitations stay: EvoPrompting released no code, so no official or paper-linked repository exists (the evaluator ports dm-clrs instead), and the paper's GPU search and training were not run.

findings: Benchmark and task: EvoPrompting (Section 4.2) evaluates on the CLRS benchmark of 30 algorithms and reports, in Appendix A.6 Table 3, the OOD accuracy and model size of the best of five discovered Triplet-GMPNN variants and of the Triplet-GMPNN baseline for every algorithm, Segments Intersect included. The paper ran no search on Segments Intersect: its Table 3 entry evaluates models found on articulation points, Graham scan and Kruskal's MST (disclosed in the Source protocol note). The task trains the CLRS encode-process-decode network (a PyTorch port of dm-clrs 2.0.3) around a candidate processor on this algorithm and scores the CLRS-30 test split. The CLRS benchmark paper (arXiv 2205.15659) and Ibarz et al. (arXiv 2209.11142) are not in .cache/primary-paper-text; I checked the CLRS facts below in the dm-clrs 2.0.3 source instead.

Data, split and sample size: CLRS-30 v1.0.0, the archive dm-clrs's dataset.py names; I checked in samplers.py that its splits are 1000 training trajectories of length 16, and 32 validation (length 16) and 32 test (length 64) samples times the algorithm's multiplier in specs.CLRS_30_ALGS_SETTINGS (64 for segments_intersect, so validation and test have 2048 samples each). The data lock lists 1000/2048/2048 samples with 4/4/4 nodes for segments_intersect.npz, and the evaluator uses 32 validation and 2048 test samples (clrs_data.spread takes evenly spaced subsets when fewer than all samples are used). dm-clrs run.py instead samples fresh training trajectories of sizes 4, 7, 11, 13 and 16 and fresh validation samples of size 16 (with randomised pos), and reads only the test split from the archive (create_samplers, checked); disclosed in the Data note, except the minor point that local validation keeps the archive's unrandomised pos (it only affects which checkpoint is restored). For this algorithm dm-clrs's SegmentsSampler ignores the length and always draws two segments (four endpoints), so every split, the archive's test split included, has 4 nodes and the test is not out of distribution; the last note says so, and the Data note, which still called the split 'OOD test' and said the original trains on sizes 4 to 16 with varied edge probabilities, was corrected.

Candidate interface: build_processor(hidden_dim) returns a torch module called once per algorithm step with node, edge and graph features, the adjacency and the previous hidden state, returning node embeddings and optionally edge embeddings, the processor's role in dm-clrs nets.py. The paper's search changed only the triplet-message function of a Triplet-GMPNN (Section 4.2); the candidate may replace the whole processor (a superset; disclosed). I compared the seed with dm-clrs processors.py (MPNN with an all-ones adjacency, message MLP [128, 128], max aggregation, layer norm, gate with bias -3, 8 triplet features, o3 with ReLU): it is the triplet_gmpnn processor, and the receipt's seed network has 263,359 parameters (258,872 in the processor), equal to Table 3's baseline size 263,359 (tests/test_clrs_training.py asserts this for all 30 algorithms; I checked the 17 sizes of this package against the cached Table 3).

Metric and scoring: the score is the mean over the algorithm's output probes of dm-clrs's evaluate metric on hard predictions; Segments Intersect has one output, intersect (graph mask: whether the two segments intersect), so the score is the F1 of the predicted flag over the 2048 test instances (threshold 0 on the logits). I compared clrs_metrics.mask_f1 with dm-clrs evaluation._mask_fn (micro-averaged tp, fp, fn; precision and recall 1 when undefined) and the probe types with dm-clrs specs.SPECS. Direction maximize, range [0, 1]; the test outputs stay in the scoring process (clrs_eval.visible_splits).

Budget: 2000 Adam updates (100 % of the paper's 2000-step search budget per child model), learning rate 1e-3, batch 32, gradient clipping 1.0, hidden size 128 (dm-clrs run.py's single-task defaults, which I checked; run.py trains for 10,000 steps), validation every 50 updates with the best checkpoint restored, one training seed (0), CPU with 4 threads, 1700 s wall-clock and 3584 MB memory limits. The paper's search used AdamW on one P100 GPU; Table 3 states no training length or hardware (Reference checks note corrected). The notes disclose that the local scores are far below and not comparable with the published ones.

Objective: the paper's search fitness is -(model size x best validation error) after 2000 steps (Section 3.3; Eval returns the lowest validation error), and the paper reports the OOD accuracy of selected models; the local score is the test score itself (in distribution for this algorithm), with a 1,000,000-parameter processor cap and no size term, so a search optimises on the reported test split (disclosed in the Objective note).

Reported values: Table 3 lists for Segments Intersect the best model Div2Mean (262,327 parameters) at 98.15 +- 0.00 %, EvoPrompting's Triplet-GMPNN at 97.40 +- 0.00 % and Ibarz et al.'s at 97.64 +- 0.09 % (baseline size 263,359); the Reference checks note quotes them correctly (compared with the cached text). The paper reports these as OOD accuracies without noting that this algorithm has no larger test size.

Seed and discrimination (receipt, not re-run by me): on 2026-10-11 (1-minute load 8.84) the seed scores 0.8617 in 27 s, below Table 3's 97.40 % as the notes say, and a processor without message passing scores 0.7156, a margin of 0.1461; an earlier run (2026-10-10) gave the identical score. The variation across training seeds was not measured. This task reaches the 2000-step cap, so the seed's evaluation takes about half a minute rather than the 3 to 7 minutes the Budget note gives as the target (the note's '2000 at most' covers this). A processor returning the wrong shape and a program importing os were rejected (receipt).

Not verified by me (no evaluator was run): the measured values in the notes and validation/clrs-checks.json (seed, reference and repeat scores, timings, memory, determinism, rejection of invalid candidates), the TFRecord conversion of scripts/prepare_clrs.py and the content digests of catalog/clrs-data-lock.json, and that the PyTorch port reproduces dm-clrs numerically (the notes say it was not cross-checked; I compared by reading the processor, metrics, hint post-processing and data options named above). The paper calls its metric 'OOD accuracy' without defining it; that it equals the CLRS evaluate score is inferred from its use of Ibarz et al.'s setup. The venue (NeurIPS 2023) is not stated in the cached arXiv v3 text.

Metadata (not a paper-relationship problem): task.json still has kind 'specification', evaluation.protocol 'specified_only', validation.level 'paper_inventory' (adapter_checks null), source_specification.implementation_status 'paper_inventory_only', requirements.hardware 'See upstream requirements and task notes.' and labels.cost 'not_run', although the suite protocol is 'recreated' and runs on the CPU; execution.notes ('... Parameter count is minimized.') describes the paper's search, not the local score. The three limitations stay: EvoPrompting released no code, so no official or paper-linked repository exists (the evaluator ports dm-clrs instead), and the paper's GPU search and training were not run.

Data, split and sample size: CLRS-30 v1.0.0, the archive dm-clrs's dataset.py names; I checked in samplers.py that its splits are 1000 training trajectories of length 16, and 32 validation (length 16) and 32 test (length 64) samples times the algorithm's multiplier in specs.CLRS_30_ALGS_SETTINGS (1 for topological_sort). The data lock lists 1000/32/32 samples with 16/16/64 nodes for topological_sort.npz, and the evaluator uses 32 validation and 32 test samples (clrs_data.spread takes evenly spaced subsets when fewer than all samples are used). dm-clrs run.py instead samples fresh training trajectories of sizes 4, 7, 11, 13 and 16 and fresh validation samples of size 16 (with randomised pos), and reads only the test split from the archive (create_samplers, checked); disclosed in the Data note, except the minor point that local validation keeps the archive's unrandomised pos (it only affects which checkpoint is restored).

Candidate interface: build_processor(hidden_dim) returns a torch module called once per algorithm step with node, edge and graph features, the adjacency and the previous hidden state, returning node embeddings and optionally edge embeddings, the processor's role in dm-clrs nets.py. The paper's search changed only the triplet-message function of a Triplet-GMPNN (Section 4.2); the candidate may replace the whole processor (a superset; disclosed). I compared the seed with dm-clrs processors.py (MPNN with an all-ones adjacency, message MLP [128, 128], max aggregation, layer norm, gate with bias -3, 8 triplet features, o3 with ReLU): it is the triplet_gmpnn processor, and the receipt's seed network has 660,164 parameters (258,872 in the processor), equal to Table 3's baseline size 660,164 (tests/test_clrs_training.py asserts this for all 30 algorithms; I checked the 17 sizes of this package against the cached Table 3).

Metric and scoring: the score is the mean over the algorithm's output probes of dm-clrs's evaluate metric on hard predictions; Topological Sort has two outputs, topo (node pointer: each node's successor in the topological order) and topo_head (node mask_one: the first node), so the score is the mean of the pointer accuracy over the 32 x 64 test nodes and the fraction of test graphs whose first node is predicted correctly. I compared clrs_metrics.probe_score and one_hot_accuracy with dm-clrs evaluation.py and the per-probe averaging with evaluation.evaluate, and the probe types with dm-clrs specs.SPECS. Direction maximize, range [0, 1]; the test outputs stay in the scoring process (clrs_eval.visible_splits).

Budget: 120 Adam updates (6 % of the paper's 2000-step search budget per child model), learning rate 1e-3, batch 32, gradient clipping 1.0, hidden size 128 (dm-clrs run.py's single-task defaults, which I checked; run.py trains for 10,000 steps), validation every 15 updates with the best checkpoint restored, one training seed (0), CPU with 4 threads, 1700 s wall-clock and 3584 MB memory limits. The paper's search used AdamW on one P100 GPU; Table 3 states no training length or hardware (Reference checks note corrected). The notes disclose that the local scores are far below and not comparable with the published ones. Training recomputes each algorithm step in the backward pass (activation checkpointing; parameter checkpoint_steps), which changes memory and time, not values (claimed; tests/test_clrs_training.py compares losses and gradients; not run by me).

Objective: the paper's search fitness is -(model size x best validation error) after 2000 steps (Section 3.3; Eval returns the lowest validation error), and the paper reports the OOD accuracy of selected models; the local score is the test score itself, out of distribution, with a 1,000,000-parameter processor cap and no size term, so a search optimises on the reported test split (disclosed in the Objective note).

Reported values: Table 3 lists for Topological Sort the best model TanhExpandTriplets (660,164 parameters) at 88.12 +- 4.71 %, EvoPrompting's Triplet-GMPNN at 76.88 +- 5.05 % and Ibarz et al.'s at 87.27 +- 2.67 % (baseline size 660,164); the Reference checks note quotes them correctly (compared with the cached text). The two Triplet-GMPNN values differ by about ten points, more than their spreads.

Seed and discrimination (receipt, not re-run by me): on 2026-10-10 (1-minute load 18.13) the seed scores 0.4719 (topo 0.2251, topo_head 0.7188) in 540 s, far below Table 3's 76.88 % as the notes say, and a processor without message passing scores 0.0491, a margin of 0.4229; the variation across training seeds was not measured for this task. A processor returning the wrong shape and a program importing os were rejected (receipt).

Not verified by me (no evaluator was run): the measured values in the notes and validation/clrs-checks.json (seed, reference and repeat scores, timings, memory, determinism, rejection of invalid candidates), the TFRecord conversion of scripts/prepare_clrs.py and the content digests of catalog/clrs-data-lock.json, and that the PyTorch port reproduces dm-clrs numerically (the notes say it was not cross-checked; I compared by reading the processor, metrics, hint post-processing and data options named above). The paper calls its metric 'OOD accuracy' without defining it; that it equals the CLRS evaluate score is inferred from its use of Ibarz et al.'s setup. The venue (NeurIPS 2023) is not stated in the cached arXiv v3 text.

Metadata (not a paper-relationship problem): task.json still has kind 'specification', evaluation.protocol 'specified_only', validation.level 'paper_inventory' (adapter_checks null), source_specification.implementation_status 'paper_inventory_only', requirements.hardware 'See upstream requirements and task notes.' and labels.cost 'not_run', although the suite protocol is 'recreated' and runs on the CPU; execution.notes ('... Parameter count is minimized.') describes the paper's search, not the local score. The three limitations stay: EvoPrompting released no code, so no official or paper-linked repository exists (the evaluator ports dm-clrs instead), and the paper's GPU search and training were not run.

evidence.supports: EvoPrompting evaluates on the CLRS benchmark of 30 algorithms (Section 4.2), of which Topological Sort is one.
EvoPrompting searched only on articulation points, Graham scan and Kruskal's MST (Section 4.2), so its Topological Sort result is a transfer evaluation, as the Source protocol note says.
The paper's search space is only the triplet representation of a Triplet-GMPNN; the local candidate may replace the whole processor (disclosed in the Objective note).

Search budget and hardware: AdamW, 2000 steps per child model on one P100 GPU (Section 4.2); the only training budget the paper states, cited in the Source protocol, Budget and (after correction) Reference checks notes.
